title: Computational Approaches to the Non-Observed Economy
book: Computational Approaches to the Non-Observed Economy: From Theory to Practice

book_parts.title: Computational Approaches to the Non-Observed Economy: From Theory to Practice

description: An open course on studying the non-observed economy with computation: what goes unrecorded and why, games between observers and the observed, estimating and forecasting a hidden quantity with honest errors, maps and networks, agent-based simulation, and policy design. 9 modules, one per chapter of the forthcoming book, with long videos, slides and browser labs.

modules.title: What is the non-observed economy?
modules.sub: Observers, boundaries and the five ways to go unseen
modules.summary: Ask a tax office, a statistics office and a card company how much an invented town produced, and you get three different answers, none of them a lie. Being observed is a relation between an activity and an observer with a purpose. We define the non-observed economy, separate it from the shadow, informal and illegal economies, draw the production boundary, and take apart its five components: underground production, illegal production, the informal sector, production for own use, and statistical omissions. Then we measure: random audits against targeted ones, surveys that stay biased however large, and a cash method whose answer moves with one assumption.
modules.goal: say who observed what, define the non-observed economy and its five components, decide what belongs inside the production boundary, and report a size with its definition, its denominator and the assumption that carries it.

card.alt: Three observation towers cast overlapping beams over a market, workshop, garden and shadowed streets.

modules.title: Theory-based and data-driven modelling
modules.sub: When the target itself is hidden
modules.summary: In most empirical work the outcome can be counted. Here the target is hidden: latent, rebuilt by someone else's model, or seen only for a few people. Studying it needs a production story and an observation story. We look at the mechanisms theory offers, five modelling objectives that are often confused, a strong association that is a weak lever, a cross-country slope with the wrong sign, and then the data side: labels and their status, provenance, coverage, timing and leakage, and a division of labour between theory and data. Forty invented countries keep every claim checkable.
modules.goal: separate the production and observation stories, match a model to its objective, recognise when an association is not a lever, audit a dataset for label status and leakage, and choose a check that matches the use.

card.alt: Gears and drawers of data cards help trace the outline of a hidden building above a toy town.

modules.title: Mathematical-economic modelling
modules.sub: Games between auditors, agents and communities
modules.summary: The observer is a player. With 2,000 invented firms, a tax office and stylised games, we write down the textbook evader and the compliance puzzle, compare audits with third-party reporting, let the tax office move first, take away its commitment in an inspection game where the fine sets the audit rate rather than evasion, and watch tipping when people copy their neighbours. Then the rules a community makes and enforces itself: how rules form, information spread across people, deterrence through the future in a market that grows from 20 to 1,280 traders, monitoring as a public good, and the dark side of community enforcement.
modules.goal: write a concealment decision and an enforcement game, compare levers inside an explicit model, explain commitment, mixed equilibria and tipping, and model community enforcement with its information, deterrence and free-riding problems.

card.alt: Shopkeepers weigh coins while a lantern-carrying observer watches a market square laid out as a game board.

modules.title: Estimating the size
modules.sub: From proxies to estimates, with honest errors
modules.summary: Fifty invented countries, thirty with a careful benchmark and twenty without: fill in the twenty and say how sure you are. We write the estimation task down, place each method in its history, fit linear models with the right shape and read their coefficients as what-if answers, then try trees, nearest neighbours, support vectors, boosting and a neural network. Random rows flatter the flexible models; whole held-out countries put the simple, well-shaped model first. Finally ranges: an ensemble's spread and quantile models are overconfident, while a Gaussian process and conformal prediction calibrated on whole countries keep their 90% promise.
modules.goal: write the size-estimation task, fit and read linear and flexible estimators, choose a check that matches the use, and report ranges with tested coverage.

card.alt: Blue bars mark measured islands while an amber estimate and uncertainty band fill a gap.

modules.title: Predicting size and trends
modules.summary: A careful estimate of the hidden share covers a year and arrives a year late, yet a ministry wants this quarter's number now. Thirty invented countries, quarter by quarter, live through a shift to digital payments, a recession and a reform. We line up four forecasters, from simply repeating the latest benchmark to anchoring on it and letting fresh indicators speak only about the change, check them with a rolling origin and real publication lags, test how much history to use, and then follow flexible forecasters into concept drift: three kinds, detected late, and adapted to by kind.
modules.goal: tell a nowcast from a forecast, beat a persistence baseline, check forecasts with a rolling origin and publication lags, name the three kinds of drift and the models each breaks, and detect and adapt to drift when the truth arrives late.

card.alt: A train leaves its last measured point behind and follows an amber beam into fog.

modules.title: Spatial dynamics
modules.sub: Where hidden activity happens, and through which links
modules.summary: One national number can hide very different maps, and the map changes the policy. On an invented country of 160 hexagonal districts with a river, a smuggling corridor, two market towns and 40 surveys, we name the support, relation, observation process and task of a spatial study, use norms and graphs (and say what an edge means), smooth where the economy is continuous and not across a border, report the distance to the evidence, and test for structure with shuffles. Then we work backwards from traces to hidden activity, list the ways that fails, validate on regions a model never saw, and compress a detailed map into a small graph of regimes.
modules.goal: choose and justify a spatial relation, use smoothness as a prior with honest borders, test spatial structure and multiple local tests, reconstruct a map from traces with a stated operator and prior, validate on unseen regions, and report fidelity and reduction for a reduced model.

card.alt: A glowing network mirrors two market towns, a river and cart routes on a hexagonal map.

modules.title: Simulating the hidden economy
modules.sub: Agent-based models from micro to macro
modules.summary: An agent-based model is an executable theory: agents with states, information, actions and rules, meeting each other under institutions, with totals computed afterwards. We design one from a question, compare decision rules (beliefs, noisy choice, thresholds, communication, learning), and build Saltmarsh, an invented town of 400 firms where hiding emerges unasked and feedback through revenue, services and trust makes a recession leave a mark and history matter. Then we connect levels, calibrate honestly when many settings fit one history, and use learning and language-model agents with validators and logs.
modules.goal: design an agent-based model from a question, choose and test decision rules, follow micro–macro feedback, validate at several levels, report the set of acceptable calibrations, and state what each scenario really assumes.

card.alt: Closed curtains spread through a seaside town as glowing loops connect shops, the town hall and public spaces.

modules.title: Designing counter-NOE policy
modules.summary: Policy against the hidden economy serves four different goals, and one instrument can help one goal while hurting another. With an invented ten-year model of audits, digital reporting and services, run through a thousand possible futures, we turn policy into a decision problem, keep six sources of uncertainty apart, compare criteria (average, bad tail, worst case, chance of reaching a target), see why learned audit rules need a little randomness and why adaptive rules need timely numbers, and then read a Pareto front, choose by weights, limits or priorities, find the assumptions behind the spread, and ask whether the recommendation changes.
modules.goal: write a policy as a decision problem, compare criteria under uncertainty, read and choose on a Pareto front, run global and decision sensitivity with the value of information, report true, observed and unseen activity separately, and plan a pilot and an adaptive rollout.

card.alt: Three policy dials overlook a town with branching future paths and a curved row of trade-offs.

modules.title: A practical guide
modules.sub: From a question to a defensible answer
modules.summary: The last module turns the course into a research practice. One invented e-invoicing reform gives six correct answers to one question, so a study must fix its estimand first: population, outcome, intervention, comparator, horizon and summary. We name task types, audiences and the cost of error, separate production, compliance and observability, then choose models from a small candidate set with a baseline, select inside the validation instead of after it, report coverage by subgroup, run a multiverse of reasonable analyses, and report so others can reproduce, check and act.
modules.goal: run a study in order from question to report, write a precise estimand, match validation to the claim, avoid selection optimism with nesting, report uncertainty by subgroup and across analyst choices, and write a reproducible, honest report.

card.alt: A path from a lantern-lit question passes measuring tools and model choices, then branches and rejoins at an open building.

episodes.title: Seen is not the same as happened
episodes.hook: Three observers, one invented town: the tax office sees 80% of what was produced, the statistics office 85%, a card company 54%.
episodes.takeaway: Observation is a relation, not a property. In the same invented town the non-observed economy is 15% of what was produced, 18% of official GDP, or 8% under the narrow shadow definition: always state the definition and the denominator.

transcript.title: One town, three answers
transcript.text: Here is a small town at night. Every light is someone producing something: a café, a repair shop, a farm, a builder. Suppose we want one simple number. How much did this town produce last year? Ask the tax office, and you get one answer. Ask the statistics office, and you get another. Ask the company that processes card payments, and you get a third. None of them is lying. Each one sees a different part of the same economy. This town is invented, so we know the truth. The tax office sees 80 percent of what was produced. The statistics office sees 85 percent. And the card company sees only 54 percent. The part that slips past all of them has a name: the non-observed economy. This course is about studying it with computation. Welcome to Computational Approaches to the Non-Observed Economy. I'm Teddy. The course follows our book, chapter by chapter. There are nine modules and twenty long videos. Every module also has a slide deck, and a lab you can run in your browser. We'll define what is missing, estimate its size, forecast it, map it, simulate it, and design policy around it. At the end, we'll put it all together into one study. You'll need some economics, probability and statistics. A little programming helps for the labs. One promise before we start. Every number in these videos comes from our own simulations, or from plain arithmetic. When a town or a country is invented, I'll say so.

transcript.title: Observation is institutional
transcript.text: Let's start with the most important idea of this module. Observation is institutional. Think about one sale in a small café. The customer knows it happened. She paid, and she drank the coffee. If she paid by card, the payment company knows that money moved. It doesn't know what was bought, or whether the café will declare it. The tax office knows only what the café declares. The statistics office knows the café's sector and size, from its register and its surveys. So, was the sale observed? The honest answer is another question. Observed by whom, about what, and for what purpose? Being observed is not a property of an activity. It's a relation between an activity and an observer. That sounds like a small philosophical point. It isn't. It decides what our models will try to estimate. Each observer also has its own purpose. The tax office wants to collect what's owed. The statistics office wants complete totals. A bank wants to manage its risk. Different purposes mean different questions, and different blind spots. So when someone tells you that something is unobserved, ask whose eyes they mean.

transcript.title: What the NOE is
transcript.text: The non-observed economy, or NOE for short, is production that belongs in the economic accounts, but is missing, or only partly there, in the data used to measure the economy. Notice what it is not. It's not one sector, one market, or one kind of behaviour. It's a measurement problem with several different causes. That's why the words in this field can be confusing. You'll read about shadow, underground, informal and illegal economies. These words grew up in different research traditions. Tax researchers studied concealed income. Labour economists studied informal jobs. Criminologists studied illegal markets. And national accountants asked a different question: are the totals complete? More than twenty years ago, statisticians from several international organisations wrote down a shared framework for this, so that countries could measure the same thing in the same way. That framework is our starting point. The words are related, but they don't name the same object. A study of the shadow economy and a study of the NOE can both be right, and still report very different numbers. Two quick examples. A worker can hold an informal job inside a fully registered firm. And an illegal sale can be watched closely by the police, while a legal sale goes unseen by the statistics office. So legal status and visibility are different things. And so are informal jobs and informal firms. Here is the practical rule. Before you estimate the size of anything, write down which activities your target includes. An algorithm will happily fit a badly defined target, very precisely.

transcript.title: The production boundary
transcript.text: The second key idea is the production boundary. It's the line that national accounts draw around what counts as production. Inside the line are goods and services made for sale. So are goods that households make for their own use, like vegetables grown for the family table. Outside the line are most unpaid services inside a household, such as cooking, cleaning and caring for children. That doesn't mean they have no value. They obviously do. It means the accounting rules leave them out, so missing them is not a measurement failure. The boundary follows the nature of production, not legality. Making and selling a prohibited product is production. Theft is not. It moves something that already exists. And some missing production involves no hiding at all. A brand new, fully legal firm can be absent from the statistics, simply because the business register hasn't caught up. For computation, the boundary works like a constraint on the target. Decide it before you train a model, not after.

transcript.title: Why it matters
transcript.text: Why should anyone care about production that nobody records? First, the national accounts. If production is missing, measured GDP is too small. And every ratio with GDP underneath it moves too: taxes, debt, productivity. Second, taxes. Modern tax systems run on information. When an employer or a bank reports your income for you, there is little room to hide. When you report it yourself, there is much more. So two people with the same true income can face very different chances to conceal it. That's a question of fairness, not only of revenue. Third, work and protection. An informal job usually comes without pension contributions, sick pay or job security. Sometimes by choice. Often because no formal job was available. Fourth, inequality. If hidden income is more common in some groups than in others, measured inequality is not the real inequality. And fifth, change. Recessions, inflation, new payment technology and new rules all shift what is hidden, and what can be seen. When the observer changes, the measured NOE can change, even if nobody's behaviour does. Here's an example. Say a country moves most shop payments onto electronic receipts. Suddenly, the statistics office sees sales that were always there. Its estimate of hidden activity drops. Did people become more honest? Not necessarily. The lamp got brighter, and it moved.

transcript.title: Lantern Bay in numbers
transcript.text: Let's make this concrete with our invented town. We call it Lantern Bay. It has 640 registered firms. It also has 900 small household businesses that never registered. Thirty producers make or sell things that are illegal. And 1,500 households grow or make goods for their own use. About a quarter of the registered firms leave some sales undeclared. Most of them are cash-heavy trades, like cafés and building work. And 40 firms opened after the statistics office last updated its register. They pay their taxes. They just aren't on its list. Before I show you the numbers, pause for a second. Which observer do you think sees the most? Now the three observers. The tax office adds up the declared sales of every registered firm. That's 80 percent of the truth. The statistics office surveys the firms on its register, and runs a household survey for the small businesses and the home production. That's 85 percent. Notice who sees the new firms. The tax office does. The statistics office doesn't. And neither of them sees the undeclared sales. The card company sees 54 percent. It sees almost none of the undeclared sales, because those are mostly paid in cash. And it can't tell which payments were declared. Here is the whole table. Rows are kinds of production, columns are observers. Each cell says how much of that row the observer records. The household survey catches about three quarters of the informal sales, because people under-report. It catches almost all of the home-grown food. And look at the illegal producers' row. Nobody records any of it. Not the tax office, not the statistics office, not the card company. So how big is the non-observed economy here? Everything the statistics office misses comes to 15 percent of what the town really produced. Measured against official GDP instead, the same missing production is 18 percent. Same town, different denominator. And if you count only concealed legal sales, the narrow shadow-economy definition, you get 8 percent. Fifteen, eighteen, eight. Three honest answers to three different questions. One more. The tax office collects 18 percent of declared sales. As a share of official GDP, that looks like 17 percent. As a share of what the town really produced, it's 14 percent.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Observation is a relation between an activity and an observer. It is not a property of the activity. The NOE is production inside the accounting boundary that the measurement system misses. It has several causes. Shadow, underground, informal and illegal describe different objects. The production boundary decides what counts. Unpaid household services are outside it. Goods made for own use, and illegal production, can be inside it. And the size you report depends on the definition and on the denominator. Always state both. So here are three questions to ask of any number about the hidden economy. Who observed? What was included? And divided by what? In this module's lab, you'll switch the observers of Lantern Bay on and off, and watch what each one records. In the next video, we'll meet the five ways production goes unobserved, one by one, and the two families of methods we use to measure them.

episodes.title: Five ways to go unobserved, and how to measure them
episodes.hook: A café skipping receipts, an unlicensed taxi, a dressmaker at home, a family's vegetables and a bakery the register missed: five reasons to go unseen.
episodes.takeaway: Five components, five traces. Random audits estimate the undeclared share (9%); the riskiest 40 firms would suggest 47%. Surveys under-report by about a fifth however large, and five points in one cash assumption move the answer by more than a quarter.

transcript.title: Five producers, five reasons
transcript.text: Five producers in Lantern Bay. A café that skips some of its receipts. A driver running a taxi without a licence. A woman sewing dresses at home for her neighbours. A family growing vegetables for its own table. And a new bakery that pays every tax, but isn't on the statistics office's list yet. All five are missing from the official picture. But for five different reasons. And each reason leaves a different trace. In this video, we'll take the five apart. Then we'll ask why activity becomes non-observed at all. And we'll finish with how to measure it, directly and indirectly.

transcript.title: Underground production
transcript.text: Component one is underground production. The activity is legal: the café is allowed to sell coffee. What's hidden is part of it, on purpose. The reasons are taxes, social security contributions, regulations or paperwork. The café is registered and reports most of its sales. The underground part is only the sales it leaves out. That's why you can't find underground production by separating registered firms from unregistered ones. It lives inside registered firms too. And it's a matter of degree. A firm chooses how much to hide, which sales, and which workers. In our models, agents will have a share, not a label. In Lantern Bay, 170 of the 640 registered firms hide something. A typical one leaves out about 30 percent of its sales. Some hide less than a tenth. Some hide more than half. Cash-heavy trades are about four times as likely to hide sales. Together, they account for three quarters of everything left undeclared. The classic explanation compares the tax saved with the expected cost of being caught. But real decisions also depend on beliefs, norms and trust, and on whether hiding is even possible. When a third party reports the transaction, like an employer reporting wages, hiding becomes much harder. Incentives and information work together.

transcript.title: Illegal production
transcript.text: Component two is illegal production. Either the product itself is prohibited, or the producer isn't allowed to make it, like our unlicensed taxi. National accounts care about production, not approval. An illegal service that people pay for is still production. Stealing a phone is not, because nothing new was made. And illegal is not the same as hidden. Some illegal markets are watched closely by the police. Some legal sales are invisible to everyone. Laws also differ between countries and over time. A product can be licensed in one country and banned in the next. So a comparison needs a stated place and year. Illegal markets also tend to run on trust and networks, because their contracts can't be enforced in court. We'll come back to networks in Modules 6 and 7.

transcript.title: The informal sector
transcript.text: Component three is the informal sector. This one is defined by the producing unit, not by hiding. Think small, household-based and unregistered, with no clear line between the business's money and the family's money. Our dressmaker isn't necessarily evading anything. Registering may cost more than it brings. Or the tax office may simply never reach her street. Formal status has costs: fees, records, taxes and rules. It also has benefits: credit, enforceable contracts and bigger customers. Whether to formalise depends on which side is heavier. And sometimes informal work is not a choice at all. When formal jobs are scarce, people create their own work. One distinction to keep. Informal employment is about the job. The informal sector is about the firm. A registered firm can employ someone informally. So a share of informal jobs is not a share of informal output. Jobs differ in hours, in scale and in productivity.

transcript.title: Own use and statistical omissions
transcript.text: Component four is household production for own use. The family's vegetables. No sale, no invoice, no wage, and so no record. Nobody is hiding anything here. The production simply leaves no trace in tax or payment data. Household and farm surveys are the right evidence, not audits. In Lantern Bay, the home growers produce under 2 percent of the town's output. And the household survey catches almost all of it, because people have no reason to hide their vegetables. Component five is statistical omissions. Our new bakery is legal, registered with the tax office, and pays everything. It's missing because the business register is out of date. Other omissions come from samples that miss fast-changing sectors, from firms that don't answer questionnaires, and from new kinds of work that no classification fits yet. This component is a warning for anyone who builds models. A missing record is not proof of hidden behaviour. Sometimes it's the observer who failed. In Lantern Bay, the 40 firms missing from the register produced almost 4 percent of the town's output. That's more than the illegal producers and the home growers put together. The five can also overlap. An informal business can hide sales, and an illegal one can employ people informally. When you measure, decide where each case goes, so nothing is counted twice.

transcript.title: Why activity goes unobserved
transcript.text: So why does activity become non-observed? Each component has its own reasons. For concealment, it's incentives and information. People hide when hiding pays, and when it's feasible. And what matters is the risk they believe in, not the official audit rate. Social life matters too. If your neighbours seem to hide income, hiding feels normal and safe. If you trust the institutions, paying feels fair. For informality, it's the costs and benefits of formal status, which change as a business grows, together with the state of the job market. For illegal production, it's prohibition, which changes both the risks and the profits. For own use, there is simply no market. And for omissions, it's the observation system itself. And the observers change the economy they watch. Make card payments more traceable, and some trade moves to cash. Start matching one kind of record, and reporting adapts. So there's no single representative agent here. Many different actors, in different institutions, make different choices. That variety is one reason this book is computational.

transcript.title: Direct measurement
transcript.text: Now, measurement. The first questions are what you're measuring, and per what. Output or jobs? A country, a region, a firm, a household? A share of official GDP, or of total production? A figure of twenty percent means nothing until those are stated. Direct methods go close to the activity. Surveys of households and firms. And audits, which compare what was reported with what is found. Matched records are a third kind of direct evidence. An employer reports a wage, and the worker declares it. A seller reports a sale, and the buyer claims it. Two independent views of the same event. When the two views disagree, you've found something. That's far stronger evidence than one source checking itself.

transcript.title: Random vs targeted audits
transcript.text: Let's run audits in Lantern Bay. The truth is that registered firms leave about 9 percent of their sales undeclared. Audit 40 firms chosen at random, and estimate the undeclared share from them. Over two thousand repeats, the typical answer is 9 percent. A single round is noisy. Most rounds land between 4 and 15 percent. Now a question before the next step. Suppose the tax office audits its forty riskiest-looking firms instead. Will its estimate of the undeclared share be too high, or too low? Now audit the 40 riskiest-looking firms instead, the way a tax office picks its cases. They hide a lot, so the audits find a lot. Extrapolate from them to the whole town, and you'd claim that 47 percent of sales are undeclared. That's five times the truth. Targeted audits are great for collecting tax. They're a terrible sample for estimating the size of anything. Random audits cost more and collect less, which is why few tax offices run them. But they're the only kind of audit that can tell you how big the problem is. Surveys have their own problem. In our household survey, people under-report their informal sales, so the typical estimate comes out about a fifth too low. And a bigger sample doesn't fix that, because the error isn't random. It always points the same way.

transcript.title: Indirect measurement
transcript.text: Indirect methods work from traces: cash demand, electricity use, gaps between spending and declared income, and models with a hidden variable. Their strength is coverage. Their weakness is that every trace has other causes. People hold cash for many reasons, and use electricity for many things. Here is a cash example. In Lantern Bay, cash sales add up to about 735 million. Part of that cash is ordinary recorded trade. The rest, we attribute to hidden trade. But how much cash does recorded trade use? Assume it's paid 35 percent in cash. Then the hidden market comes to about 280 million. Assume 30 percent instead, and it grows to about 355 million. Assume 40 percent, and it shrinks to about 200 million. Five points in one assumption, and the answer moves by more than a quarter. That assumption needs evidence of its own. And no algorithm removes that need. A flexible model can learn a published estimate very well, without showing that the estimate is the truth. The strongest evidence combines sources with different weaknesses: surveys, audits, matched records and traces. Agreement means more when the sources fail in different ways.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. There are five components: underground, illegal, informal sector, own use, and statistical omissions. Different causes, different traces, different evidence. Activity becomes non-observed through incentives, information, institutions and the observation system. And it reacts when the observers change. Measurement starts with a target, a unit and a denominator. Direct methods have sampling and honesty problems. Indirect methods have assumption problems. And targeted audits are not a sample. And always ask which assumption is doing the work. In the cash method, one assumption moved the answer by more than a quarter. In the lab, you'll sort Lantern Bay's producers into the five components, and see which observer records each one. Next module: theory-based and data-driven modelling, and what to do when the thing you want to predict is never observed itself.

episodes.title: When the target itself is hidden
episodes.hook: Two models of a published estimate score 4.5 and 8 points. Against the truth, both are off by about 8.
episodes.takeaway: The flexible model's good score came from recognising countries it had seen. Ten more points of digital payments go with 5.2 fewer points of hidden activity across countries; pushing them up by ten points, all else fixed, cuts it by 0.3.

transcript.title: Two models, three scores
transcript.text: Here are forty countries, sixteen years each. For every country and year, someone has published an estimate of its hidden economy. We train two models to predict that published estimate. One is flexible: a random forest that sees everything we have. The other is simple, and only uses variables that theory says matter. Test them on a random quarter of the rows. The flexible model is off by about 4.5 points. The simple one, by 8. Now test them on ten countries they have never seen. The flexible model's error jumps to almost 7 points. The simple one barely moves. And here's the twist. These countries are invented, so we know the true hidden share. Against the truth, both models are off by about 8 points. So which number would you report? That question is what this module is about.

transcript.title: Two stories
transcript.text: Welcome to Module 2: theory-based and data-driven modelling. In most empirical work, the thing you're explaining can be measured. People argue about why unemployment changes, but they can count the unemployed. Here, the target itself is hidden. It's latent, or reconstructed by somebody's model, or observed only for a few people. So every study of the hidden economy needs two stories. A production story: how hidden activity arises. And an observation story: how evidence about it reaches us. Theory is good at the first. Data are good at testing both. In this video, we look at what theory brings, and what each kind of model is for. The plan: first the mechanisms theory gives us, then the five things a model can be for, then a trap about prediction and policy, then what makes a model theory-based, and finally back to our two models.

transcript.title: Mechanisms
transcript.text: Start with concealment. Economists have long modelled crime and tax evasion as a choice: people compare what they gain from hiding with what they expect to lose if caught. That gives hiding an economic logic. But real people don't know the audit probability. They act on the risk they believe in, shaped by experience, advisers and rumours. Information is part of the mechanism too. When an employer reports your wage, there's little to hide. With value added tax, one firm's sale is another firm's purchase, so their reports can be checked against each other. Digital invoices and payments add more traces. But data only deter if the tax office can link them and use them. Then there's social life. People learn from their neighbours what is normal and what is risky. And trust matters: people pay more willingly when they see taxes as fair and services as worth it. Informal firms need a different story: the costs and benefits of registering, and the jobs that are actually available. Illegal markets need another: prohibition, secrecy and trusted networks. And statistical omissions need a story about the observer: registers, samples and classifications. A theory of the hidden economy must include the observation process, not only the production process. Notice that no single mechanism covers all of this. Hiding sales, running an unregistered shop, selling something illegal and being missed by a register are different processes. A model has to be built for the process you're studying.

transcript.title: Five objectives
transcript.text: Before choosing a model, choose the objective. There are five, and they're often confused. Measurement asks how big the hidden economy is, now or in the past. It's judged by how credible the reconstruction is, and how honest its uncertainty. Explanation asks why it exists, or why it changed. It needs mechanisms, and it's judged by whether those mechanisms account for the patterns we see. Prediction asks what will happen next, using only what's known today. It's judged on data the model has never seen, in time order. Simulation asks how individual choices add up. It's judged by whether it reproduces patterns at both the small and the large scale. And policy asks what would happen if we changed something. That needs a counterfactual, which is much more than a good prediction. In our forty countries, the five look like this. Measurement: how big was the hidden share in country twelve last year? Explanation: why is it falling there? Prediction: what will it be next year? Simulation: how do millions of individual choices add up to that number? And policy: what happens if country twelve doubles its audits? A model can be excellent at one of these and useless at another. A random forest can predict well and explain nothing.

transcript.title: Prediction is not policy
transcript.text: Here is why prediction is not policy. In our forty countries, places with more digital payments have less hidden activity. Across countries, ten more points of digital payments go with about 5 fewer points of hidden activity. So, should a government push digital payments up by ten points? Pause for a moment, and guess how much hidden activity would fall. We can actually run that experiment, because we built this world. Force digital payments up by ten points, and keep everything else the same. Hidden activity falls by about a third of a point. Not five. A third of one. Why? Because in this world, strong institutions drive both. They bring digital payments, and they bring enforcement and trust. Digital payments mostly ride along. Draw it as arrows. Institutions point to digital payments. Institutions also point to enforcement and trust, and those point to hidden activity. Digital payments have only a thin arrow of their own. Any variable with a strong common cause can look like a lever. Theory is what tells you which arrows exist. A model that predicts well will happily use digital payments as a clue. That's fine for prediction. It's wrong for policy.

transcript.title: Theory-based models
transcript.text: So what makes a model theory-based? Not equations. The structure comes from an economic argument, made before the model sees the data. A linear regression isn't automatically theory. And a machine-learning model can carry a lot of theory: which variables enter, which signs are allowed, which actions are possible. The classic evasion model is a good template. One person chooses how much income to report. Then you can add beliefs, norms, trust, third-party reports, or repeated audits, and solve it with a computer. Firms work the same way. Register or not, declare how much, pay workers formally or not, accept cards or cash. Theory says why each choice matters. Data say how much. The strength of theory is interpretation. Its weakness is identification. Here's a warning from our own world. In this world, raising taxes makes people hide more. We built it that way. Five extra points of tax adds about a point of hidden activity. Yet across countries, higher-tax countries hide less. Five more points of tax go with almost 9 fewer points of hidden activity. Same world, opposite signs. Strong institutions raise both taxes and compliance. The correlation tells you about institutions, not about taxes.

transcript.title: Proxies
transcript.text: Some of the oldest size estimates were theory-based too. Currency demand methods assume that hidden trade needs extra cash, beyond what normal habits explain. Electricity methods assume that production needs power, recorded or not. And latent-variable models combine several causes and several indicators at once. Each made a hidden quantity approachable. Each also leans on a proxy with other causes. Cash depends on banking, interest rates and habits. Power depends on technology and climate. Latent-variable models tried to fix that by listening to many causes and many indicators at once: tax burden, regulation and unemployment on one side; cash, power and working hours on the other. That spreads the risk across several proxies. But it raises new questions: is the hidden quantity really identified, and in what units is it measured? The published estimate in our forty countries is built that way. It leans on cash use. It follows the truth closely, with a correlation of zero point nine two. But it's off by about 6 points on average. It's too high where cash is common, and too low where it's rare.

transcript.title: Name tags
transcript.text: Back to our two models. Why did the flexible one look so good on random rows? Because a country's years look almost alike. From one year to the next, the hidden share has a correlation of zero point nine four. A random split puts a country's neighbours in training and its other years in the test. The forest learns each country's quirks. Population, for example, is fixed for each country, so it works like a name tag. On new countries, the name tags are useless, and the error grows by half. The simple model has no name tags, so its score barely moves. That's honest. But it isn't more accurate against the truth. So report both scores, and say which one matches your use. If you'll apply the model to countries it has never seen, the random-split score is the wrong one to quote. And there's a deeper problem. Both models learned the published estimate, not the hidden economy. We'll take that apart in the next video.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. The hidden economy needs two stories: how activity arises, and how evidence about it is produced. Theory brings mechanisms: incentives and information, norms and trust, the costs of formality, prohibition, and the observer itself. Measurement, explanation, prediction, simulation and policy are different objectives, judged in different ways. A strong association can be a weak lever. And a correlation across countries can have the opposite sign to the mechanism. In the lab, you'll build the forty countries yourself, train both models, and switch between random and country splits. Next: ground truth, leakage, and how to make theory and data work together.

episodes.title: Ground truth, leakage, and making theory and data meet
episodes.hook: A published estimate says a reform cut hidden activity by 8 points. The reform's true effect was 3.5.
episodes.takeaway: A model trained on an estimate learns the estimate (8.3 points from the truth on new countries, against 6.5 for the estimate itself). The split must match the use, and last year's value (2.4 points) beat a random forest (3.4).

transcript.title: A reform the estimate misreads
transcript.text: Half of our forty countries introduce electronic invoicing in year ten. Every sale gets a digital record. The published estimate reacts strongly. In those countries, it says the hidden economy fell by 8 points. Because this world is invented, we can rerun it without the reform. The reform's true effect was about 3.5 points. The estimate more than doubled it. Nobody lied, and nothing was miscalculated. Pause and think: what went wrong? The estimate reads cash use. The reform pushed people from cash to cards, so the estimate's input fell, even where hiding didn't. The reform changed the observation process, not only behaviour. This video is about seeing that kind of trap before it bites.

transcript.title: Data are made by institutions
transcript.text: Start with a mindset. A dataset is not a neutral picture of the economy. It's a product of institutions and behaviour. Tax records exist because rules require reports. Registers exist because firms register. Payment data exist because people pay through a particular system. And the same institutions that create the hidden economy decide what data exist to measure it. So a data infrastructure has to connect five things: the target, the observation process, where each variable came from, who is covered, and when each value became known. We'll go through them one at a time, then look at what flexible models add, and finish with a division of labour between theory and data.

transcript.title: An estimate is not ground truth
transcript.text: First, the target. It might be a national estimate, an audit finding, a count of informal jobs, or a risk flag on a transaction. These are different objects. And many of them are estimates, not observations. A published shadow-economy series may itself come from a currency model or a survey. Train a model on such a series, and the model learns the series. In our world, a forest trained on the published estimate ends up about 8 points from the truth on new countries. The published estimate itself is about 6.5 points from the truth. The student is no better than its teacher. If we could train on the truth, the same forest would be about 7 points off. That's the gap we lost to the label, before any modelling choice. Audit data have a different problem, which we met in Module 1. Audits target risky cases, so a model trained on them partly learns how auditors choose. So label every target with its status. Directly observed, rebuilt from records, reported in a survey, produced by a model, or imputed. And carry that uncertainty forward. A useful trick is to combine a little direct evidence, like a survey in a few places, with broad indirect indicators that cover everywhere. The direct evidence anchors the level. The broad indicators spread it across places and years. Neither alone can do both jobs.

transcript.title: Provenance
transcript.text: Second, where each variable came from. Every source sees only a projection of the economy. Tax returns see what was declared. Card data see card payments, and nothing paid in cash. Keep a record of each variable's history: who collected it, how its definition changed, what was done to it, and when it became available. Here's why. Suppose a statistics office changes how it classifies self-employment in a given year. The series jumps. A model that doesn't know about the change will learn the jump as if it were behaviour. Without that history, the reform at the start of this video is uninterpretable. Recorded sales rise. Is that less hiding, more production, better records, or all three? Linked records are especially valuable: an employer's report against a worker's, a buyer's invoice against a seller's. They add information about the same event, not just more columns. But check that your confirmations are independent. Three variables computed from the same tax return are one source, not three.

transcript.title: Coverage, timing and leakage
transcript.text: Third, coverage. The process that hides activity can also keep it out of the dataset. Registered firms are easier to see than unregistered ones. Card payments are easier to see than cash. A billion card payments can describe the card network perfectly, and still say little about the trade that moved to cash. We saw it in Lantern Bay. The card company had detailed records of more than half the town's output, and almost nothing on the undeclared sales, which were paid in cash. Fourth, timing. Values arrive late and get revised. If a model trains on revised numbers, or on audits that finished later, it's using the future. That's leakage. It can also sneak in through preprocessing, filling in missing values, building features, and splitting at random. Here's a common version. You fill in missing values using the average of the whole dataset, test rows included. Now every training row carries a little information from the test set. Or you build a feature from a country's average over all years, then test on its later years. The future has quietly entered the past. In our forty countries, the flexible model scored 4.5 on random rows, and almost 7 on new countries. Same model, same data, a different question. So the split must match the use. Forecasting means testing on later years. Transfer means testing on whole new countries. Risk scoring means testing on new firms. Maps mean testing on new regions. And remember how much data you really have. Our panel has 640 rows. But with years this alike, it behaves more like forty stories than six hundred and forty.

transcript.title: What flexible models bring
transcript.text: Now, what do flexible models bring? They can learn shapes and interactions that nobody wrote down. Cash may mean something different where banks are scarce. Their discipline is out-of-sample testing. Fit on some data, judge on other data. And match their flexibility to the real amount of information, with regularisation and simple baselines. And always run a simple baseline. Here's one for forecasting: just use last year's published value. On the last four years of our panel, that's off by about 2.4 points. The random forest, trained on the earlier years, is off by about 3.4. The one-line baseline wins. Complexity has to earn its place. Know what each feature is. It may be a cause, a consequence, a trace of the observation system, or just a control. A feature can predict well because it names a country, or a reporting system. Even the fact that a value is missing can be a name tag. That's fine if you'll only ever predict for the same countries under the same systems. It breaks the moment you move to a new country, or the reporting system changes. Explanation tools, like SHAP values, describe what a model uses. They don't tell you what would happen if you changed that feature. Important to the model is not the same as a policy lever. And relationships drift. A model trained before electronic invoicing learned a world that no longer exists after it. Treat a data-driven model as something you monitor, not something you finish. A practical habit: keep watching the gap between your model and any fresh direct evidence, like a new survey or a round of random audits. When the gap grows, the world has moved.

transcript.title: Theory and data together
transcript.text: So how do theory and data work together? Give each the job it's good at. Theory should fix the target, the actors, and what each of them knows. It should say how a policy reaches behaviour. And it should impose accounting identities, legal limits and feasibility. Data should learn the sizes, the shapes, the thresholds and the interactions that theory can't pin down. And data should decide whether extra complexity earns its place. Here's an example. Theory says that third-party reporting makes hiding harder. It doesn't say whether the effect is a straight line, whether there's a threshold, or whether it depends on firm size. That's what data are for. Or the effect of digital payments may depend on whether the tax office can actually link payment records to tax returns. Theory names the interaction. Data measure it. Then validate against the objective. And when a model fails, read the failure. Failing after a reform says the observation process changed. Failing in low-trust countries says trust is missing from the model. For our reform, the fix is to model the observation process explicitly. Let the estimate know that cash use changed for reasons other than hiding. And use a counterfactual. Compare with similar countries that didn't reform, or with a simulation of the same world without the reform, the way we did here. That's the loop: theory proposes, data test, failures teach, and theory is revised. Neither side gets the last word.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. A dataset is made by institutions. Record each target's status, and each variable's history. A model trained on an estimate learns the estimate. It can't be more right than its label. Coverage depends on how data are generated, not on how much there is. And the test split must match the intended use. Theory fixes the target, the actors, the information and the constraints. Data learn the shapes. Failures teach you which part was wrong. And a one-line baseline is the first test any complex model has to pass. In the lab, you'll switch on the reform, and watch the published estimate, the truth, and your models disagree. Next module: games between auditors and the people they audit, written down as mathematics.

episodes.title: The enforcement game
episodes.hook: Double the fine for evasion: evasion dips, then drifts most of the way back, and the tax office audits about two fifths less.
episodes.takeaway: At realistic audit rates, more third-party reporting cut hiding by a fifth while doubling audits cut it by under 4%. Without commitment the fine sets the audit rate, and with copying one audit rate supports two very different worlds.

transcript.title: Double the fine
transcript.text: A tax office doubles the fine for evasion. What happens to evasion? In our simulation, it drops at first. Then, slowly, it creeps most of the way back. What changed for good is the tax office. Once the fine doubled, it audited about two fifths less. Nobody planned that. It falls out of the logic of a game. And that's what this module is about: the observer is a player too.

transcript.title: The observer is a player
transcript.text: Welcome to Module 3: mathematical-economic modelling. I'm Teddy. In Module 1 we saw that observers change the economy they watch. Game theory is the tool for that. It treats the tax office and the firms as players, each reacting to the other. Computation helps when the algebra runs out: many different firms, beliefs, learning, neighbours. We write down the rules, and let the computer play the game. Why computation? Solving one firm's problem takes a line of algebra. Solving two thousand different firms, who learn and copy each other, has no neat formula. A simulation shows the whole path, including the surprises along the way. Today: one firm's choice, a whole population of firms, a tax office that moves first, one that can't, and what happens when people copy their neighbours.

transcript.title: The textbook evader
transcript.text: Start with the textbook evader. Every number in this example is invented. The tax rate is 20 percent. If a firm hides a sale and gets caught, it pays the tax, plus a surcharge of the same size. So hiding one euro of tax gains one euro if you're not caught, and costs one extra euro if you are. A firm that only counts money will hide everything, unless its chance of being caught is above one half. Real audit rates are a few percent, not fifty. So this model says almost everyone should hide almost everything. Yet most firms pay most of their taxes. Economists call this the compliance puzzle. The model is missing something. Several things, actually. Hiding gets harder the more you hide. You can't hide what someone else reports for you. Some people simply won't cheat. And people act on the risk they believe in, not the official one.

transcript.title: Two thousand firms
transcript.text: So let's add those, and build a population. Two thousand invented firms. Three in ten never hide anything. For the rest, hiding gets more expensive the more they hide, and part of their sales is reported by others, like card companies and business customers. Each firm picks the amount that pays best for it. We let the computer solve two thousand small problems, and add them up. With two percent of firms audited, about 16 percent of all sales are hidden. Now double the audits, to four percent. Hidden sales fall by less than four percent of what they were. Instead, keep the audits, and let third parties report thirty more points of each firm's sales. Hidden sales fall by more than a fifth. At realistic audit rates, in this world, information beats inspection. What you can't hide matters more than how often you're checked. Notice what the computer added. Each firm's problem is easy. But the total depends on how costs and third-party shares are spread across firms, and that needs the whole population.

transcript.title: Moving first
transcript.text: Now the tax office. Suppose it moves first. It announces an audit policy, sticks to it, and the firms respond. Game theorists call this a leader and followers. The office knows how firms will react, so it can choose its policy with that reaction in mind. Each extra audit costs money, and brings back some tax. The office keeps auditing until one more audit costs more than it recovers. That gives two regimes. When audits are cheap, it pays to audit enough that nobody hides at all. When audits are expensive, the office accepts some hiding, on purpose. In our population, with cheap audits the office goes all the way to deterrence. With expensive audits, it stops at about ten percent, and accepts that about fourteen percent of sales stay hidden. These audit rates are far above real ones, because our fine is mild and our firms count only money. The point is the shape of the decision, not the levels. That second regime is uncomfortable, but common. A tolerated level of evasion can be the result of a calculation, not of neglect. Moving first is valuable. But only if the promise is believed. Once everyone complies, the office is tempted to stop auditing. And firms know it. Why not just make the fine enormous? Because fines are limited by law and by fairness. Audits make mistakes, and an enormous fine on an honest firm is a disaster. Huge fines also make bribes more attractive. And the office has a second lever besides audits: information. Third-party reporting, electronic invoices, matching records. In the model, that lever changes what firms can hide, not just the chance of being caught.

transcript.title: Both move at once
transcript.text: So what if the office can't commit? Then both sides move at once. The office decides whether to audit. The firm decides whether to evade. Neither sees the other's choice. Try to find a stable pair. If the office never audits, firms evade. If firms evade, the office audits. If it audits, they comply. If they comply, it stops auditing. Round and round. The way out is randomness. The office audits just often enough that evading stops paying. Firms evade just often enough that auditing still pays. And here's the twist. The amount of evasion is set by the office's costs and gains, not by the fine. The fine only sets how often the office must audit. That's what we saw at the start. In our simulation, firms and the office learn by trial and error. Before the change, about 6 percent of firms evade, and the office audits about 30 percent. Then the fine doubles. Evasion drops to about 2 percent. But the office learns that audits find less, and audits less. Evasion drifts back up, to about 5 percent. Meanwhile, the audit rate settles near 17 percent. About two fifths lower than before. Evasion doesn't come all the way back, because our simulated firms make small mistakes. But most of the dip is gone. These are stylised games, so don't read the levels literally. Read the logic. A bigger stick can mean fewer inspections, rather than fewer evaders. And commitment pays. In this game, an office that can credibly promise its audit rate loses half as much per firm as one that can't. Notice the dip after the change. A study that measured evasion one year after the fine doubled would call it a big success. Two years later, the effect is mostly gone. Timing is part of the result.

transcript.title: Copying the neighbours
transcript.text: So far, each firm decided alone. But people watch each other. If your neighbours seem to evade, evading feels normal, and safer. Let's build two thousand agents. Each one has a private wish to evade, which audits push down. And each one leans towards what the others are doing. Before we run it, a question. If we turn the audits up and then back down along the same path, will evasion retrace its steps? Now we turn the audit rate up slowly, starting from a world where most people evade. Evasion stays high, and then suddenly collapses, at about five and a quarter percent audits. Now turn the audits back down. Compliance holds, much longer than you'd expect. Evasion only returns below four percent. So at five percent audits, there are two possible worlds. In one, most people evade. In the other, almost nobody does. Which one you get depends on history. Without the copying, the same agents give one smooth curve, with about 43 percent evading at five percent audits. Two lessons. Cutting enforcement can be cheap to do, and expensive to undo. And two countries with the same policy can sit in different equilibria, so comparing them can mislead you. Taking this to data is hard. Neighbours look alike for many reasons: shared rules, shared customers, shared shocks. Copying is only one of them. Separating them needs careful designs, which is a theme for Module 6. The same goes for the other parameters. Concealment costs can be estimated from audit data. Beliefs about audit risk come from surveys. Every parameter in these games needs its own evidence.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. The textbook evader hides everything at realistic audit rates, so real behaviour needs more: costs of hiding, third-party reports, morals and beliefs. In our population, more third-party reporting cut hiding far more than doubling the audits. A tax office that moves first can choose its tolerated level of evasion. One that can't commit plays a game where the fine sets its audit rate, and its own costs set the evasion. And when people copy each other, the same policy can support two very different worlds. In the lab, you'll play the audit game against learning firms, double the fine, and watch what adapts. Next video: what happens when there's no tax office at all, and the community enforces the rules itself.

episodes.title: When communities enforce the rules
episodes.hook: Twenty traders with no tax office stay 99% honest. At 320 traders only 37% do. A shared record brings it back.
episodes.takeaway: Deterrence through the future works in small, stable groups and fades as they grow, unless a shared record takes over. Monitoring is a public good: five members acting alone catch a cheat 16% of the time, against 43% if they coordinate.

transcript.title: Twenty traders, then 320
transcript.text: Here is a market of twenty traders. No tax office, no courts. If you cheat a partner, the news spreads, and people stop trading with you. In our simulation, 99 percent of these traders stay honest. Now grow the market to 320 traders. Same kind of people, same rules. Only 37 percent stay honest. Give them a shared record of who cheated whom, and honesty goes back to 99 percent. Morals didn't change. Information did. This video is about rules that a community makes, watches and enforces by itself.

transcript.title: Governance without a government
transcript.text: In the last video, the government was a player with a clear job. Here, nobody has that job. The rules come from the population itself. That isn't only history. Think of merchant associations, villages sharing a pasture or a fishing ground, cooperatives, informal labour markets, and online platforms with reputation scores. Often there is a formal state too. Community rules can replace it where it doesn't reach, or work alongside it, explaining and enforcing its rules locally. For the non-observed economy this matters a lot. Much informal activity isn't ungoverned. It's governed by people other than the tax office. One warning before we start. Community compliance and legal compliance are different things. An informal job can be perfectly accepted locally, and still break labour law. And the reverse holds too. A deal within the law can still break a community rule, like an obligation to help a neighbour. So community governance isn't automatically lawful, efficient or fair.

transcript.title: How rules form
transcript.text: How do community rules form? Sometimes by explicit agreement. A rule is adopted when enough support gathers behind it. But support is rarely equal. Older members, big traders, or people who control something essential can carry more weight. Other rules just grow. A practice that keeps working gets copied, and becomes expected. One that keeps failing fades. And support alone doesn't make a rule strong. It also needs legitimacy, it must be enforceable, and applying it can't cost too much. A rule everyone likes, but nobody can check, is weak. A rule few people like, enforced by a powerful group, can be strong. An invented example. Lantern Bay's fishers agree to sell only at the morning market, where everyone can see the catch and the price. Selling on the side is cheaper for one fisher, but it hides the catch from everyone else. The rule works as long as most fishers support it, the morning market is easy to watch, and breaking it gets noticed. Change any of those, and the rule weakens.

transcript.title: Nobody sees everything
transcript.text: Next, information. In a community, nobody sees everything. One person saw the payment. Another knows the amount. A third knows whether the seller had a licence. A deal becomes known if at least one trusted path brings the right pieces together. Five witnesses, each with a thirty percent chance of passing it on, give an eighty-three percent chance that it gets out. And not everyone needs to know. It's enough that the right people do: a market elder, a lender, the members who would refuse to trade. Credibility matters too. A rumour from a known liar counts for little. A report from someone who saw the deal, and has nothing to gain, counts a lot.

transcript.title: The shadow of the future
transcript.text: Now enforcement. Cheating a partner pays once. Being shut out costs you every future trade. So the rule holds when the one-off gain is smaller than the chance of being found out, times what you'd lose: any immediate penalty, plus the value of all your future trade. In our market, a trader who values the future the way we assume loses about nine periods of trade if everyone shuts them out. But gossip has a reach. We built a friendship network, eight friends each, and let news travel two steps. With twenty traders, about four in five hear about a cheat. With three hundred and twenty, fewer than one in ten. With twelve hundred and eighty, two in a hundred. Fewer people who hear means fewer partners lost, so the threat shrinks. Honesty falls from 99 percent, to 37, to under 3. Before we look at the fix, pause. What would you add to a market of twelve hundred and eighty traders to bring honesty back? A shared record restores it, at any size. That's one way to read the history of registers, credit bureaus and reputation systems: they replace gossip when communities grow. It also explains a pattern in the hidden economy. Small, stable groups can sustain a lot of informal trade on trust. As they grow and become anonymous, that trust needs formal support. Notice that the shared record doesn't have to belong to a government. A traders' association, a cooperative or a platform can keep it. What matters is that news reaches the people who would refuse to trade.

transcript.title: Watching is a public good
transcript.text: There's a catch. Watching others costs time and effort. But when you catch a cheat, everyone benefits, not just you. So each member watches a bit less than the group would want. Economists call this a second-order free-rider problem. The rule is a public good, and so is enforcing it. We let members choose how much to watch, each one doing what's best for themselves. With five members, the chance of catching a cheat is about 16 percent. If they coordinated, it would be 43. With a hundred members, it's 70 percent instead of 99. And each member watches about a third as much as with five. Communities that last tend to fix this on purpose. Monitoring in turns. A shared fund for enforcement. Rewards for credible reports. Sanctions that start small and grow. And a cheap way to settle disputes. Why start small? Because people make honest mistakes, and observers get things wrong. A warning keeps a useful relationship alive. Big penalties are kept for those who repeat. Governments face the same problem with each other. Two tax offices both gain when a cross-border deal is traced, and each prefers the other to pay for it. In a simple version, acting alone they trace 56 percent of such deals. Coordinating, 75. That's the case for information-sharing agreements.

transcript.title: The dark side
transcript.text: Community enforcement has a dark side, and a model should include it. Reports can be false. Rivals can be accused. Information from marginalised people can be ignored. And a wrong reputation can follow someone for years. Powerful members can define the rules to protect themselves. And punishment can be excessive, or aimed at outsiders. So when you model a community, don't assume it's efficient or fair. Make those properties outcomes you measure. And watch what happens when formal rules arrive. A new registration system can weaken the community's own enforcement before the formal one works. Whether that happens is an empirical question. A model is a way to ask it carefully.

transcript.title: From theory to data
transcript.text: How do you take this to data? Write down what the model needs, and ask where you could measure it. Who can observe whom. How fast and how reliably news travels. How big the sanctions are, and how much membership is worth. And what people believe about all of it. Some of these come from surveys and experiments. Some from network data. Some only from careful fieldwork. We'll build the network side in Module 6, and full agent-based models in Module 7. Experiments help too. In public-goods games in the lab, many people pay a cost to punish free riders, and that changes how others behave. How strongly, differs between places and groups. So parameters measured in one community don't travel automatically. And platform data, where they exist, record ratings, complaints and exclusions directly. That's community enforcement leaving a trace.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Many rules in the hidden economy are made and enforced by communities, not governments. Community compliance is not legal compliance. Rules need support, legitimacy, enforceability and low cost. Information is spread across people, and a deal is known when one trusted path brings it together. Deterrence comes from the future. It works in small, stable groups, and fades as they grow, unless a shared record takes over. Watching is a public good, so it's underprovided. And community enforcement can be unfair, so measure fairness rather than assuming it. In the lab, you'll grow the market, change how far gossip travels, and add a shared record. Next module: estimating the size of the hidden economy, from proxies to estimates with honest errors.

episodes.title: The estimation task and linear models
episodes.hook: Fill in twenty countries nobody has studied. A straight line predicts a hidden economy below zero for five country-years.
episodes.takeaway: A logistic link removed the negative estimates and cut the error on new countries from 4.9 to 4.2 points. Tax alone goes with almost 15 fewer points per 5 points of tax; with controls the sign flips to about +2, near the true +1.

transcript.title: Fill in twenty countries
transcript.text: Here are fifty invented countries. For thirty of them, the statistics office has done a careful study of its hidden economy. For the other twenty, nobody has. Your job is to fill in the twenty. And because we invented this world, we can check every answer against the truth. We start with the simplest tool there is: a straight line through the data. It does surprisingly well. But for five country-years, it predicts a hidden economy smaller than zero. Change one thing, the shape of the link between the line and the share, and the negative shares disappear. The error drops too, from about 5 points to about 4. That's the spirit of this module. Every estimator carries assumptions. Good estimation is choosing them on purpose.

transcript.title: Three videos, one world
transcript.text: Welcome to Module 4: estimating the size of the non-observed economy. I'm Teddy. This module has three videos. This one sets up the task and the linear models. The next one covers trees, neighbours, margins and boosting. The last one covers neural networks, honest uncertainty, and a fair comparison. All three use the same invented world, which we call the Archipelago. Fifty countries, twelve years each.

transcript.title: The estimation task
transcript.text: Let's write the task down carefully. A unit can be a country in a year, a region, a sector or a firm. For each unit, there's a hidden share we never see directly. Multiply that share by an observed scale, like official GDP, and you get the hidden economy in money. Say what the share is a share of. In the Archipelago, it's a share of everything produced, hidden or not. As we saw in Module 1, dividing by official GDP gives a bigger number for the same activity. What we do see comes in three kinds. Causes: things that push activity into hiding, like tax burden, weak enforcement or low trust. Indicators: traces that hidden activity leaves, like extra cash, a gap between spending and declared income, or electricity that recorded output can't explain. And benchmarks: careful estimates for a few units, from audits, special surveys or the statistics office's own completeness checks. A general estimator balances three wishes at once. Explain the indicators. Agree with the benchmarks where they exist. And stay plausible, for example by changing smoothly from year to year, and staying between zero and one. In the Archipelago, the benchmark exists for thirty countries, and it's close to the truth. Our models learn from those thirty, and estimate the other twenty. That's a realistic setting. Careful benchmarks are expensive, so they exist for some countries and not others. The rest need a model that carries the measured level across.

transcript.title: A short history
transcript.text: This task has a long history, and it helps to know it, because modern models inherit its assumptions. The earliest estimates read money. If hidden trade needs cash, then cash beyond what normal habits explain points to hidden activity. Everything depends on what counts as normal. Later came models with a hidden variable, which link several causes and several indicators to one unobserved size. Others compared what households spend with what they declare, or electricity with recorded output. Direct surveys and audits got better too, with careful wording for sensitive questions. And statistics offices developed their own methods, built into the national accounts. The main lesson of that history: no single method is a reliable benchmark. They measure different parts of the hidden economy, under different assumptions. So the best evidence triangulates.

transcript.title: Linear models and shape
transcript.text: Now, the linear model. Predict the hidden share as a weighted sum of the inputs. The computer picks the weights that make the errors on the thirty countries as small as possible. Its strength is that you can read it. Each weight says how the prediction moves when one input moves, and the others stay fixed. How does it pick the weights? It squares each error and adds them up. Squaring punishes big misses more than small ones, and it makes the best weights easy to compute. To report how good a model is, we'll use the average size of the miss, in points of hidden share. Four points means that a typical estimate of, say, twenty percent could really be sixteen or twenty-four. Its first weakness is shape. A share lives between zero and one. A straight line doesn't know that. In the Archipelago, the straight line predicts negative hidden shares for five country-years. The lowest is minus three percent. The fix is a link function. Fit the line to the log-odds of the share, then squeeze the result back between zero and one. Small shares stay small, but never negative. With the link, the lowest prediction is about three percent, and the error on the twenty new countries falls from 4.9 points to 4.2.

transcript.title: A sign that flips
transcript.text: The second weakness is interpretation. Let's look at the tax burden. Before the numbers, a quick guess. Across countries, do higher taxes go with more hidden activity, or less? Fit the share on tax alone, across countries. Five more points of tax go with almost fifteen fewer points of hidden activity. Add enforcement, trust and the other causes, and the sign flips. Now five more points of tax go with about two points more. We built this world, so we know the truth: about one point more. The controlled model has the right sign, and the right order of size. A coefficient answers the question: what if this input changed and the others didn't? Leave out the others, and you answer a different question. And inputs that move together, like enforcement and trust, make individual weights unstable, even when the predictions are fine. Report predictions with confidence. Read single weights with care.

transcript.title: Regularisation and two checks
transcript.text: With many inputs and few countries, a model can chase noise. Regularisation pushes weights towards zero, unless the data insist. The lasso goes further: it sets some weights exactly to zero, so it also chooses inputs. In our world, it kept ten of the eleven inputs, and dropped bank access. Its cousin, ridge regression, shrinks all the weights a little instead of zeroing some. It helps most when inputs move together. Here, it didn't help. The lasso's error on new countries was about 5 points, a little worse than the plain model with a link. Regularisation earns its keep when inputs are many and data are scarce, and in this world they aren't scarce enough. One more check. We estimated the linear model's error two ways: holding out random rows, and holding out whole countries. Both said about 5 points. A simple model can't memorise a country's quirks, so the two checks agree. Keep that in mind for the next video, where they won't.

transcript.title: Look at the data first
transcript.text: Before you trust any of this, look at the data itself. Where does each variable come from? Which countries are missing which years? Is the benchmark a measurement, or someone else's model? Plot each input against the benchmark. Look for breaks in series, for countries that sit far from the rest, and for inputs that are almost copies of each other. Check the benchmark too. Is it the same kind of estimate in every country? A benchmark built from a survey in one country and from tax audits in another isn't one target, it's two. And look at time. A series that jumps in one year, in one country, is more often a change in how it was measured than a change in the economy. In the Archipelago, the currency ratio depends on cash habits as much as on hiding. A model that leans on it will be wrong wherever habits differ. That kind of knowledge doesn't come from the fit. It comes from knowing how the data were made.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. The estimation task has a hidden share, an observed scale, causes, indicators, and benchmarks for some units. A good estimator explains the indicators, respects the benchmarks, and stays plausible. History says no single method is a reliable benchmark, so triangulate. Linear models are readable. Give them the right shape with a link function, read coefficients as what-if answers with everything else fixed, and expect unstable weights when inputs move together. In the Archipelago, a linear model with a logistic link estimates the twenty new countries within about four points. In the lab, you'll build the Archipelago's linear model, switch the link on and off, and watch a coefficient flip as you add controls. Next: trees, neighbours, margins and boosting. They're more flexible. Are they better?
