episodes.title: Trees, margins, neighbours and boosting
episodes.hook: A decision tree's first question found the enforcement threshold we built into the world, with no hint.
episodes.takeaway: Trees, neighbours, support vectors and boosting look best on random rows. On the twenty new countries the linear model with a link won (4.2 points), ahead of support vectors (5.5) and boosting (6.0).

transcript.title: The tree's first question
transcript.text: We asked a decision tree to estimate the hidden economy of our fifty invented countries. Its very first question was about enforcement. Is enforcement below zero point three five? If yes, the hidden share is much higher. That's exactly the threshold we built into this world. Nobody told the tree. It found it in the data. Flexible models can discover shapes we didn't write down. The question for this video is what that flexibility costs.

transcript.title: Four families
transcript.text: Welcome back to Module 4. This is video two: trees, margins, neighbours and boosting. Same task as before. Thirty countries with a careful benchmark, twenty without, and we score on the twenty against the truth. We'll meet four families of models, then put them side by side, with two different ways of checking them. A reminder of what makes this world hard. The hidden share jumps when enforcement is weak. Cash matters more where banks are scarce. And each country has quirks no input explains.

transcript.title: Decision trees and depth
transcript.text: A decision tree asks a sequence of yes or no questions. Each question splits the data on one input, at the value that makes the two groups as different as possible. At the end of each path, it predicts the average of the countries that landed there. To choose each question, the tree tries every input and every cut point, and keeps the one that reduces the error the most. Then it repeats inside each group. After the enforcement question, our tree asks about the spending gap on one side, and the currency ratio on the other. You can read it like a flowchart. The danger is depth. Let the tree grow, and it ends up with one country-year per leaf. Its error on the training data drops to zero. But on new countries, deep trees are no better than a tree four questions deep. The extra questions only memorise noise. So the depth is chosen by checking on held-out data. In our world, four questions was best. Trees have a big advantage for this field: they need no scaling, they handle odd distributions, and a shallow one can be shown to a minister on one slide.

transcript.title: Nearest neighbours
transcript.text: The second family is the nearest neighbours. To estimate a country, find the countries that look most like it, and average their benchmarks. It's intuitive. It's how many experts actually reason. This country looks like those countries, so its hidden economy is probably similar. Two choices matter. How many neighbours: in our world, ten worked best. And what similar means: inputs measured in different units have to be put on the same scale first. If you measure tax burden in percent and population in people, population will decide every neighbour. Scaling makes each input count on a comparable footing. Its weakness is that every input counts as much as every other, unless you weight them. Irrelevant inputs make countries look alike for the wrong reasons. It also can't extrapolate. A country more extreme than any in the training data gets the average of the most extreme ones it knows, which is too moderate.

transcript.title: Support vector regression
transcript.text: The third family is support vector regression. It fits a tube around the data, and ignores errors smaller than the tube's width. Only the points outside the tube shape the model, so it's quite robust to small noise. With a kernel, the tube can bend, so it isn't limited to straight lines. It's sensitive to scaling, and to two or three settings that control the tube's width and how much it can bend. Those settings need careful checking too. In our world, its random-row score was about five points, close to the best. On whole held-out countries, it rose to about six. Keep those two numbers in mind.

transcript.title: Boosting
transcript.text: The fourth family is boosting, and in practice it's often the strongest. Gradient boosting libraries like XGBoost are everywhere in applied work. The idea is to build many small trees in a row. Each new tree looks at the errors left by the trees before it, and tries to fix a little of them. Add trees, and the training error keeps falling, towards zero. The error on new countries falls quickly, and then stops improving after about a hundred trees. That's why boosting needs early stopping, a small learning rate, and shallow trees. Each one limits how much noise it can learn. The learning rate is how much of each new tree's correction we keep. Small steps, many trees, and a stop when held-out error stops falling: that's the standard recipe. Boosted models are hard to read directly, but you can ask them questions. Hold everything fixed, slide enforcement from low to high, and watch the average prediction. Below about zero point three five, the boosted model predicts about thirty-seven percent hidden. Above it, about twenty-four. It found the threshold too. Shuffle one input at a time, and see how much worse the predictions get. The currency ratio matters most, then enforcement, then the spending gap.

transcript.title: The check decides the winner
transcript.text: Now the comparison. First, the way many studies do it: hold out random rows, train on the rest, and measure the error. On that check, the flexible models look best. Boosting scores about 4.7 points, the support vector model 5.0, and the linear model 5.0. Before the next result, pause. Which model do you expect to do best on the twenty countries it has never seen? On the new countries, against the truth, the order changes. The linear model with a logistic link is best, at about 4.2 points. The support vector model comes next, at 5.5. Boosting gets 6.0. The tree and the neighbours both about 6.9. The random-row check flattered the flexible models. A country's years look alike, so random rows let a model recognise a country it has already seen. Holding out whole countries tells a much more honest story. On that check, boosting's score rises to about 5.3, the neighbours' to 6.0, and the tree's to 6.4. With only thirty countries to learn from, a model with the right shape beat models that could learn any shape. That's not a law. With more countries, or stronger non-linear effects, the ranking could flip. Why does memorising a country help on random rows? Because a country's twelve years share its institutions and its quirks. Seeing eleven of them makes the twelfth easy. Seeing none is the real task.

transcript.title: How to choose
transcript.text: So which should you use? Here's a practical way to choose. Start with a linear model, with the right link and sensible inputs. It's your baseline, and it's readable. Then try a flexible model. If it beats the baseline on whole held-out countries, not just random rows, use what it learned. Look at its partial dependence for shapes like thresholds. Use the same held-out countries for every model, the same inputs, and a similar effort tuning each one. Otherwise you're comparing effort, not models. And sometimes you can put what the flexible model found back into the simple one. We tried it: a weak-enforcement flag in the linear model. In our world, it didn't help. The error went from 4.2 to 4.4 points. The threshold is real, but with thirty countries, other errors dominate. Testing an idea is cheaper than believing it.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Trees ask yes-or-no questions and can find thresholds. Their depth must be chosen on held-out data. Neighbours average similar countries, so scaling and the choice of inputs decide what similar means. Support vector models fit a tube, and need careful settings. Boosting builds many small trees that fix each other's errors. It's strong, but it needs early stopping, and questions like partial dependence to be read. And the way you check decides the winner. Random rows flattered the flexible models. Whole held-out countries put the simple, well-shaped model first. And testing an idea, like putting the threshold into the simple model, is cheaper than believing it. In the lab, you'll grow a tree question by question, change the number of neighbours, and run both checks yourself. Next: neural networks, error bars you can trust, and an honest comparison of everything.

episodes.title: Deep and probabilistic estimators, and an honest comparison
episodes.hook: Five 90% ranges, checked on twenty unseen countries: one held the truth 37% of the time, two kept their promise.
episodes.takeaway: A small neural network was unstable with thirty countries. Ranges from an ensemble's spread covered 37% and quantile boosting 52%; a Gaussian process and conformal prediction calibrated on whole countries covered 90%.

transcript.title: Ranges that keep their promise
transcript.text: Five models give an estimate for the same invented country, each with a ninety percent range. In theory, each range should contain the truth nine times out of ten. We checked them on twenty countries none of them had seen. One range contained the truth only thirty-seven percent of the time. Another, fifty-two percent. Two of them got it right: ninety percent, as promised. A number without an honest range can mislead. A range that isn't honest misleads more. This video is about telling them apart.

transcript.title: Three parts
transcript.text: Welcome to the last video of Module 4. I'm Teddy. We'll start with neural networks, then move from single numbers to ranges, and end with a fair comparison of everything we've built in this module. Same setting as before: thirty countries with a careful benchmark, twenty without, and the truth hidden in our pocket to check every answer.

transcript.title: Neural networks need data
transcript.text: A neural network stacks simple units in layers. Each unit takes a weighted sum of its inputs and bends it. Stack enough of them, and the network can represent almost any shape. That power has a price: data. A network has many weights, and with few examples it fits noise easily. Training adjusts all the weights a little at a time, to reduce the error. Tricks like weight penalties, and stopping before the training error hits zero, keep it from memorising. We trained the same small network on six, twelve, eighteen, twenty-four and thirty of the Archipelago's benchmark countries. Its error on the new countries jumped around: about 29 points with six countries, 8 with twelve, 19 with eighteen, and about 6 with thirty. The linear model stayed between about four and five and a half points the whole way. With thirty countries, deep learning has little to learn from. It shines with many units, like regions, firms or satellite images, and with careful regularisation. Even then, keep the target in mind. A network trained on a published estimate learns the estimate, just like any other model. Networks can also predict a range directly. Instead of one number, the network outputs a centre and a spread, and is trained to make the truth likely under that spread.

transcript.title: Why ranges
transcript.text: Now, ranges. A single number hides how unsure you are. Twenty percent, give or take two, and twenty percent, give or take twelve, lead to different decisions. Uncertainty has several sources. The benchmark itself is noisy. The model's form might be wrong. And a new country can be unlike any country in the training data. The first source, noise in the benchmark, never goes away with more data. The last one, a country unlike the others, is the most dangerous, because a model can't know what it hasn't seen. A probabilistic estimator gives a whole distribution, or at least a range. There are several ways to get one, and they don't capture the same sources. We tried five on the Archipelago, each asked for a ninety percent range, and counted how often the truth fell inside, on the twenty new countries.

transcript.title: Ensembles, quantiles, a Gaussian process
transcript.text: First, an ensemble. Train many boosted models on resampled data, and take the spread of their predictions. That spread only measures how much the model wobbles. It contained the truth only thirty-seven percent of the time. The ranges were narrow, and they ignored the noise and the differences between countries. Second, quantile boosting. Train one model for the low end and one for the high end. Better, but still only fifty-two percent. A quantile model is trained with a lopsided error. For the high end, missing below costs nineteen times more than missing above, so the model learns a line that only one country in twenty should cross. Both were tuned on countries they had seen, and they were overconfident about countries they hadn't. Third, a Gaussian process. It's a model that comes with its own uncertainty, which grows as a new country gets further from the ones it knows. It covered the truth ninety percent of the time, with ranges about nineteen points wide. That honesty isn't guaranteed. A Gaussian process trusts its own assumptions about smoothness. Here they happened to fit. In another world, they might not, so its coverage must be checked too.

transcript.title: Conformal prediction
transcript.text: Fourth and fifth, conformal prediction. It's a simple recipe that works with any model. Fit the model on part of the data. On the rest, measure how big its errors are. Then make every range wide enough to cover ninety percent of those errors. That's all. No assumptions about the shape of the errors. The only assumption is that the held-out data look like the new data, and that assumption is exactly where it can go wrong. The crucial choice is what you hold out. Hold out random rows, and the errors come from countries the model already knows. Those ranges contained the truth eighty-two percent of the time on new countries. Too narrow. Hold out whole countries instead, and the recipe measures the errors that matter for new countries. Those ranges covered ninety percent, as promised. They're wide, about twenty-four points. That's honest. With thirty countries, that's how much we really know about a new one. So an honest range has to be calibrated on the same kind of question you'll ask it. Here, that means whole countries. When you report a range, report three things: its width, how often it covered the truth on a held-out check, and what was held out. A range without its check is just a decoration.

transcript.title: Every model side by side
transcript.text: Let's put everything side by side. For each model: its error on new countries, whether it gives an honest range, how readable it is, and how much data it needs. The linear model with a link: the best point estimate here, about four points, and fully readable. Add a conformal range calibrated on countries. The Gaussian process: about four and a half points, with its own honest range in this world. Less readable, and slow on very large data. Boosting: about six points here, but strong when data are many and effects are tangled. Readable through partial dependence. Needs a calibrated range. The tree and the neighbours: easy to explain, weaker here. The neural network: needs far more data than we have. And for policy, remember Module 2. A good estimate of the size is not a model of what would change it. Predictive accuracy is one goal among five. No model wins everywhere. What holds up is a process: look at the data, design the check to match the use, compare honestly, and report ranges you've tested. And if two models are close, prefer the one you can explain, check and maintain. In this field, someone will ask why the estimate moved, and you'll need an answer.

transcript.title: A checklist
transcript.text: Here's that process as a checklist you can use on real data. First, explore the data and its origin. Where did each variable and each benchmark come from, and which ones are themselves estimates? Second, design the estimation. Which units, which target, which split matches the use, and which baseline must every model beat? Third, compare a small set of models on that split, with the same inputs and the same budget for tuning. Fourth, interpret. Read coefficients and partial dependence, check whether the shapes make economic sense, and report the range with its tested coverage. And remember the label. If your benchmark is a model, everything you build inherits its assumptions. Write all of this down before you look at the results on the held-out countries. Choosing the check after seeing the scores is one of the easiest ways to fool yourself.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Neural networks need many more units than thirty countries. With little data, they're unstable. Ranges matter as much as point estimates. An ensemble's spread and quantile models were overconfident here. A Gaussian process, and conformal prediction calibrated on whole countries, were honest. The best point estimate came from the simplest model with the right shape. The best practice came from a process, not a model. In the lab, you'll ask each model for a ninety percent range, and watch how often the truth lands inside. Next module: predicting the size and its trend over time. Forecasting something you can't see.

episodes.title: Forecasting something you can't see
episodes.hook: A careful estimate arrives a year late. Reusing it is off by about 2.8 points; a regression trained in calm years misses by 8 in a recession.
episodes.takeaway: Anchoring on the latest benchmark and letting indicators speak only about the change stayed near 2 points (2.2 overall). Random held-out quarters flattered the regression (3.4 points against 4.9 checked honestly): use a rolling origin and real publication lags.

transcript.title: The number arrives late
transcript.text: The most careful estimate of a country's hidden economy usually arrives late. In our invented world, it covers a whole year, and it's published a year after that year ends. But a ministry wants this quarter's number, now. What do you do? The simplest answer: reuse the latest estimate. Across thirty invented countries and eight years, that's off by about 2.8 points. A model that reads fresh indicators, trained in calm years, does better while things stay calm. Then a recession hits, and it's off by eight points. A third approach, which keeps the old estimate as an anchor and lets the indicators say only how much has changed, stays around two points, even in the recession. This video is about forecasting a quantity nobody observes directly, and checking those forecasts honestly.

transcript.title: Adding time
transcript.text: Welcome to Module 5: predicting the size and the trend of the non-observed economy. I'm Teddy. In Module 4 we estimated the size for countries without a benchmark. Now we add time. We want the hidden share this quarter, and next year, using only what's known today. Our world is the Archipelago again, now quarter by quarter. Thirty invented countries, forty-eight quarters, with three things that happen along the way: a shift to digital payments, a recession, and a reform.

transcript.title: Two traditions
transcript.text: Forecasting has two long traditions, and both matter here. The statistical one started with smoothing: give recent observations more weight, and let the level and the trend adapt. Then came models that use past values and past errors, and state-space models. A state-space model fits this field beautifully. It says there's a hidden process that evolves over time, and we only see it through noisy measurements. That's exactly the situation of the hidden economy. The econometric tradition added long-run relationships between series, models that switch regime in a crisis, and panel models that pool many countries. Factor models went further. They compress dozens of indicators into a few. And nowcasting changed the question. Instead of a fixed annual dataset, the information grows release by release, at different frequencies, with different delays. Forecasting becomes a matter of using each piece the moment it arrives. Researchers brought these tools to the hidden economy: long panels of estimates studied as a persistent process, dynamic versions of the cash models, and long-run relationships built into hidden-variable models. The common thread is respect for time. Values persist, they react to shocks with delays, and the rules of the game can change.

transcript.title: What the analyst sees
transcript.text: Here is what our analyst sees. A careful annual benchmark, close to the truth, but published a year late. And four indicators, every quarter, almost at once: the cash ratio, an electricity gap, unemployment, and the share of digital payments. Mixed frequencies are normal. Some indicators are monthly, some quarterly, the benchmark yearly. And the indicators have problems of their own: they get revised, and their definitions change. So there are two targets. A nowcast is this quarter's hidden share. A forecast looks a year ahead. Both have to be made from today's information only. And there's a catch for checking. The truth is never observed. In practice, you score last year's nowcasts when the benchmark finally arrives. In our world, we can also score them against the truth.

transcript.title: Three forecasters
transcript.text: Let's line up the forecasters. The first is persistence: the latest published benchmark, unchanged. It's the baseline every model must beat. It sounds naive, but hidden shares move slowly, so last year's careful number is often close. In calm periods here, it was off by only about one and a half points. The second is smoothing with a trend. It extrapolates the benchmark series. Here, it did slightly worse than persistence, about 3.3 points. Trends in a short annual series are noisy. The third is a regression. Learn how the indicators relate to the benchmark in past years, then apply that to this quarter's indicators. Each past quarter gets the benchmark of its year as a label, so the model learns from hundreds of quarter-country pairs, even though the benchmark is annual. In calm periods it's as good as anything, about one and a half points. But in the recession, its error jumps to eight. Overall, it's the worst of the three, at about five. Why? Because it learned levels. Unemployment rose beyond anything in the training years, and the link between cash and hiding changed in half the countries. A model of levels has nothing to hold on to.

transcript.title: Anchor and update
transcript.text: The fourth forecaster keeps the best of both. Take the latest benchmark as the level. Then use the indicators only to estimate how much has changed since that benchmark's year. Call it anchor and update. It's the state-space idea in plain form: a precise but old measurement, plus timely but noisy signals about the change. An example with made-up numbers. Say last year's benchmark for a country was twenty percent. Since then, unemployment rose and cash use moved in a way that, in past years, went with one more point of hiding. The nowcast is twenty-one. When the next benchmark arrives, the anchor moves to it, and the update starts again from there. Errors can't pile up for long. Its overall error is about 2.2 points. It stays near two through the technology shift and the recession, and rises to about three during the reform. A year ahead, everything gets harder. Persistence and anchor and update are both about three points off. The regression, about six. Ranges should widen with the horizon too. For anchor and update, the typical miss grew from about two points for this quarter to about three for next year. A forecast without a range hides that. When the target is hidden and arrives late, an old but careful measurement is worth more than it looks. Use new signals for the change, not for the level.

transcript.title: Checking forecasts honestly
transcript.text: Now, how should forecasts be checked? The tempting way is to hold out random quarters and train on the rest. Before the numbers, guess. Will the random check make the regression look better, or worse, than it really is? Better. With random quarters held out, the regression scores about 3.4 points. Checked the honest way, it's about 4.9. For boosting, the gap is wider: 2.9 on random quarters, 5.3 honestly. Random holes let a model peek at the quarters around the hole, including the future. The honest check is called rolling origin. Stand at a date, use only what was known then, forecast, move forward one quarter, and repeat. It's slower, and it's the only check that matches how forecasts are used. And respect the publication lag. A benchmark for a year can't be used until it was actually published. Training on it earlier is leakage, even if the number is in your file. In real life you can only score against the benchmark, a year later. That's slow, and noisy. Keep a log of every forecast you made, with its date, so you can score it honestly when the truth, or the best estimate of it, arrives.

transcript.title: How much history
transcript.text: How much history should a forecaster use? More data usually helps. But old data come from a world that may have changed. We tried windows of two, three and five years, and all the history. For the regression, shorter windows made things worse, not better. With two years of data, its recession error doubled. It saw too little to learn anything stable. For anchor and update, a short window helped a little, especially during the technology shift. It only learns changes, which need less data, and recent changes are the relevant ones. So the right amount of history depends on what the model learns. Test it with the same rolling check, don't assume it.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Forecasting the hidden economy means forecasting a quantity that arrives late, if at all. Persistence is the baseline. A regression on levels did well in calm times and failed in the recession. Anchoring on the latest benchmark and updating with indicators was the most robust. Check with a rolling origin, respect publication lags, and test how much history to use. In the lab, you'll run all four forecasters through the Archipelago's shocks, and change how much history they see. Next video: flexible forecasters, and what happens when the world they learned stops existing.

episodes.title: Deep forecasts and concept drift
episodes.hook: After a switch to digital payments, the forecaster's favourite clue lost most of its meaning: shuffling cash added over 12 points of error before, under 4 after.
episodes.takeaway: Trees cannot extrapolate (boosting was 9 points off in the recession), and each kind of drift breaks a different model. With an annual benchmark a year late, the first drift alarm rang three years after the shift began: watch faster signals.

transcript.title: The favourite clue loses its meaning
transcript.text: In fifteen of our invented countries, people switch to digital payments. So does part of the hidden trade. Before the switch, the cash ratio was by far the most important input of our boosted forecaster. Shuffle it, and the error grew by more than twelve points. After the switch, shuffling it adds less than four. The model's favourite clue lost most of its meaning. Nobody told the model. That's concept drift: the world a model learned changes under it. This video is about noticing, and adapting.

transcript.title: Four questions
transcript.text: Welcome back to Module 5. This is video two: flexible forecasters and concept drift. We'll look at what machine learning and deep learning bring to forecasting, the three kinds of drift that matter in this field, how to detect them, and how to adapt.

transcript.title: Flexible forecasters
transcript.text: Machine learning forecasters treat the past as features. Recent values, lags, rolling averages, and the indicators, all fed to a model like gradient boosting. Typical features include last quarter's value, the change since last year, a seasonal pattern, and how old the latest benchmark is. Designing them is most of the work. They can learn interactions and thresholds. But trees have one hard limit: they can't predict outside the range they've seen. In our recession, unemployment went higher than in any training year. The boosted forecaster's error jumped to about nine points. It simply had no leaf for that world. A tree predicts by averaging similar past cases. If no past case had unemployment this high, it averages the most extreme ones it has, which were milder. So it under-reacts, exactly when reacting matters most. Deep learning offers sequence models, like recurrent networks and transformers, that read a whole history and learn their own features. They need many long series to learn from. Thirty countries with a dozen annual benchmarks are not enough. They become useful with monthly data, many regions, or many firms. Whatever the model, the label problem from Module 2 stays. A forecaster trained on a published estimate forecasts the estimate.

transcript.title: Three kinds of drift
transcript.text: Now, drift. The book distinguishes three kinds, and our world has one of each. A technology shift. Digital payments jump in fifteen countries. Cash falls for reasons that have nothing to do with hiding, and hidden trade starts using digital channels too. The meaning of the cash indicator changes. A behaviour shift. The recession raises unemployment, and hiding rises by about two and a half points on average. The relationships may hold, but the inputs move into new territory. A regulation shift. Ten countries introduce e-invoicing. Hiding truly falls, by about three and a half points, and at the same time payments move to cards. Behaviour and observation change together. In the real world, these come in many forms. Mobile money and payment apps, platform work, new reporting rules, crises, inflation. Each one can change what hiding looks like, or what our indicators mean. Each one hurts different models. The regression on levels suffered most in the recession, about eight points. Persistence suffered most after the reform, about four. Anchor and update stayed between about two and three throughout.

transcript.title: Detecting drift
transcript.text: How do you notice drift, when the truth is never observed? The natural signal is each new benchmark release. When it arrives, score last year's nowcasts against it. If the errors grow, raise an alarm. A common recipe adds up the errors as they arrive, and raises the alarm when the running total drifts too far from zero. It catches a slow drift that no single error would reveal. We did that for the regression, with an alarm when the error doubles. The shift to digital payments began in quarter twenty. Pause for a moment. When do you think the first alarm went off? In quarter thirty-two. Three years after the shift began. The benchmark is annual and arrives a year late, so the evidence of drift arrives late too. The scored errors tell the story. About one and a half points for the calm years, then two, then almost five. As the recession began, between five and six, and a year into it, over ten. By the time the alarm rang, the model had been wrong for a long time. When the target is slow to arrive, drift detection has to use faster signals. There are several. Watch whether models that should agree start to disagree. Watch relationships between indicators, like cash against card payments. And fund small, fast direct evidence, like a quarterly survey or a round of random audits, as an early warning.

transcript.title: Adapting
transcript.text: Once you've noticed drift, how do you adapt? The obvious move is a shorter training window, so old relationships fade. As we saw in the last video, that can backfire. The regression got worse with less history. Better moves depend on the kind of drift. For a technology shift, change the inputs: the cash ratio needs a companion, the digital share, and their meaning must be re-estimated after the shift. For a behaviour shift into new territory, prefer models that extrapolate sensibly, like ones built on changes rather than levels, or with a structure from theory. For a regulation shift, model the observation process explicitly, as we said in Module 2, and compare with similar countries that didn't change. Two more tools help in every case. Retrain on a schedule, not only when something breaks. And keep several models trained on different windows, so you can see when they start to disagree. And in every case, anchor on fresh direct evidence whenever it arrives. That's what kept anchor and update steady here. Picture the reform year from the analyst's chair. The cash indicator drops sharply in ten countries. Before reading it as less hiding, check what else changed: the reform moved payments to cards. Hold the nowcast near the anchor, flag it, and wait for direct evidence.

transcript.title: Explanations expire
transcript.text: Drift also changes explanations. Tools like SHAP values, or the simpler shuffle test we used, describe what a model relies on. Before the technology shift, our boosted model leaned on cash above everything. After it, cash mattered about a third as much. And the model's error rose to 4 points, up from 2.3. So explanations have an expiry date. Recompute them after any shift, and never present an old one as a description of today's economy. The same is true of the coefficients of a simple model. A weight estimated before a shift describes the old world. Re-estimate it, and say which period it comes from. And remember, as in Module 4: important to a model is not the same as a lever for policy.

transcript.title: A routine
transcript.text: Here's a practical routine for forecasting the hidden economy. Keep a persistence baseline. Use a rolling-origin check with real publication lags. Prefer models that anchor on the latest careful estimate. Log every benchmark release, and score last year's nowcasts against it. Watch faster signals for drift. And when you find drift, ask which kind it is before you change the model. Report forecasts with ranges, and say how the range was checked. A forecast of something nobody sees deserves more humility, not less. And write down, in advance, what would make you distrust your own forecast. A new payment system, a reform, a crisis. When one of those happens, check the model before you publish its number.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Flexible forecasters learn interactions, but trees can't extrapolate, and deep models need far more series than thirty countries. Drift comes in three kinds: technology, behaviour and regulation. Each one breaks different models. Benchmarks that arrive late make drift detection late, here by three years, so watch faster signals. Adapt to the kind of drift, anchor on fresh evidence, and recompute explanations after every shift. In the lab, you'll switch the three shifts on and off, watch the alarms, and see which forecaster survives. Next module: where hidden activity happens, and through which links. Spatial dynamics.

episodes.title: Shadows have neighbours
episodes.hook: Three maps of one invented country, each averaging 22% hidden: evenly spread, along a corridor, or around two market towns.
episodes.takeaway: Moran's I was 0.86 on the Mainland, but a survey method alone produced 0.26, and a shuffled map still showed 7 'significant' local clusters. Picking audits by network exposure found a hider a third of the time, against one in eight at random.

transcript.title: Same average, three maps
transcript.text: Here are three maps of the same invented country. In every one of them, the hidden share of the economy averages 22 percent. In the first map, hiding is spread evenly. In the second, it follows a smuggling corridor. In the third, it gathers around two market towns. A national estimate can't tell these apart. It's the same number every time. But they call for different policies. Patrol a corridor, inspect two markets, or improve services everywhere. Where hiding happens, and through which links, is part of the answer. This module is about seeing that structure.

transcript.title: The Mainland
transcript.text: Welcome to Module 6: the spatial dynamics of the non-observed economy. I'm Teddy. Our world zooms in on one country of the Archipelago. We call it the Mainland. It has 160 districts on a hexagonal map. A river splits it into two provinces. The West introduced e-invoicing, so it hides less. In the East there's a smuggling corridor from a border crossing to the port, two market towns, and hills full of self-employment. Careful surveys exist in 40 districts, mostly around the capital in the West. Everything else has to be estimated.

transcript.title: Name four things
transcript.text: Spatial analysis starts from a simple observation: nearby things tend to be more related than distant ones. But nearby can mean many things. Two districts can be neighbours on the map. Two countries can be close because their institutions are alike. Two firms can be close because they share an owner or trade every week. So before any model, name four things. The support: where is the process defined? Districts, firms, or transactions. The relation: who counts as close? The observation process: how does hidden activity leave traces? And the task: describe, predict, reconstruct, or simulate. Two warnings come with maps. Change the size of the regions, and the patterns you find can change. And a pattern among regional averages need not hold for the people or firms inside them.

transcript.title: Distance and bandwidth
transcript.text: The first way to represent space is a norm. Put every district in a feature space, and measure how far apart they are. The features can be coordinates, or the economy: cash use, self-employment, income, digital payments. The choice of distance says what similar means. When features are correlated, a distance that accounts for that stops one idea from being counted twice. When they mix numbers and categories, you need a distance built for mixed data. Distances turn into weights through a kernel, and the kernel has a bandwidth. Let's estimate the 120 unsurveyed districts from the 40 surveyed ones, weighting by economic similarity. With a tiny bandwidth, each estimate leans on one or two lookalikes, and the error is about 5.2 points. At the best bandwidth, it's 4.7. With a huge bandwidth, every survey counts equally. The error climbs to 9.2, almost exactly the error of the plain average. Which neighbours should count? Five nearest on the map gave an error of 4.8. Five nearest in the economy, also 4.8. A distance that mixes both did better, at 4.4. A norm also lets relationships change across space. A local regression fits its own coefficients around each district. Useful, but a map of local coefficients is not a map of causes.

transcript.title: A firm network
transcript.text: The second representation is a graph. Nodes are units, and edges are relations: shared borders, similar profiles, trade, ownership, or movement of workers. Graphs come with a toolbox. Who is central, how clustered the network is, and which groups trade mostly among themselves. One graph is often not enough. Geography, transactions, ownership and social ties are different layers. Merging them can invent paths that don't exist, so say what an edge means. Here's a firm network we invented. Three hundred firms in fifteen trading communities. In three of those communities, most firms hide sales. Elsewhere, few do. Fifteen hiders have already been caught. The tax office can audit thirty more. Who should it pick? Picking at random finds a hider in about one audit in eight. Picking the firms located closest to known hiders, about one in five. Picking by network exposure, how close a firm is to known hiders through its trading links, finds a hider in a third of the audits. The communities weren't geographic, so the map missed them. One caution: the edges most likely to be missing are cash deals and informal subcontracting. A missing link is not proof of independence.

transcript.title: Smoothness and borders
transcript.text: A graph also lets you measure smoothness: add up the squared differences between connected districts. Small means neighbours look alike. That sum is a useful regulariser. But smoothness is an assumption, not a law. Borders, reforms and special zones create real jumps. Our river is one. Let's take a cheap, noisy estimate for every district, and smooth it over the map. Right at the river, the true step between the provinces is 6.4 points. Smoothing across the river shrank it to about four. Cutting the edges that cross the river kept a step, though it overshot, at 8.7 points. And near the river, the error fell to 1.6 points, down from 1.8. Smooth where the economy is continuous. Let the model jump where the rules change.

transcript.title: Distance from the evidence
transcript.text: Distance can also be an indicator in its own right. Distance from a tax office, a bank, or a border can stand for enforcement, transaction costs, or how well statistics reach a place. On a globe, straight-line distance is a start. Inside a country, travel time and road access usually mean more. And a nearest-neighbour graph can quietly create very long edges for remote places, so look at it. In networks, distance is the shortest path. A firm can be one ownership step from a known shell company, and far away on the map. One distance deserves a place in every report: how far a district is from the nearest surveyed district, in the economy's terms. For the quarter of districts closest to a survey, our neighbour estimates were off by about 1.7 points. For the farthest quarter, about 10.5. Every one of the farthest was in the East. Distance from the evidence is a warning light. It tells you when a model is extrapolating, which a standard confidence interval often doesn't.

transcript.title: Moran's I and local clusters
transcript.text: Now, how do you test whether a map has structure at all? The classic statistic is Moran's I. It asks whether connected districts deviate from the mean in the same direction. For the Mainland's hidden shares, Moran's I is 0.86. To judge it, shuffle the values across the map and recompute. None of 999 shuffled maps came close. The evenly spread map from the start scores about zero. The corridor map, 0.70. The market-town map, 0.59. Here's a trap. We made a map with no hidden structure at all, but the East's survey method reads three points high. Moran's I jumped to 0.26, and again, no shuffle came close. Spatial structure in the measurements is not the same as spatial structure in the hidden economy. Local statistics break the map into clusters: high districts among high neighbours, low among low, and outliers. The Mainland has 36 high clusters, 55 low ones, and no significant outliers. Before the next number, guess. If we shuffle the map completely, how many districts will still look like significant clusters? Seven. With 160 tests at the five percent level, some false hot spots are guaranteed. Local maps are exploratory, and multiple testing has to be reported. Finally, a dependent map can enter a regression in two ways. Neighbours' hidden shares can affect each district directly, or the errors can be correlated because something spatial is missing. They mean different things, and cross-sectional data often can't tell them apart.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. A national number hides very different maps, and the map changes the policy. Name the support, the relation, the observation process and the task. Norms measure similarity, graphs encode relations, and both need a stated meaning. Smooth where the economy is continuous, not across borders. Report the distance to your evidence. And test structure with shuffles, remembering that measurement methods can create it. In the lab, you'll explore the Mainland's map, change who counts as a neighbour, and hunt for hot spots, real and false. Next video: turning traces on a map back into the hidden activity that made them.

episodes.title: From a map to a model
episodes.hook: Read cash withdrawals as hiding and eight bank towns hold 81% of it. In the invented truth they hold about 5%.
episodes.takeaway: The raw inversion was off by 4.4 points and light smoothing by 2.2. A wrong observation operator raised the error to 11.6, while deleting 30% of graph links left it at 2.2. Holding out whole regions doubled the map-neighbour error (2.3 to 4.6).

transcript.title: Where cash becomes visible
transcript.text: Here's the Mainland's map of cash withdrawals. The brightest districts are eight towns with banks. Read it as a map of hiding, and those eight towns hold 81 percent of all hidden activity. In our invented world, we know the truth. They hold about five percent. People from the countryside travel to town to withdraw cash. A trace shows where activity becomes visible, not where it happens. This video is about working backwards, and checking the result honestly.

transcript.title: Four steps
transcript.text: Welcome back to Module 6. This is video two: from a map to a model. We'll reconstruct a hidden map from its traces, list the ways that fails, validate spatial predictions properly, and compress a detailed map into a small model of regimes.

transcript.title: The inverse problem
transcript.text: Spatial analysis of the hidden economy is often an inverse problem. We see traces, and we want the activity that produced them. Write the traces as the hidden map passed through an observation operator. In our world, a rural district withdraws 80 percent of its cash in the nearest town, and only 20 percent locally. If we know that operator, we can invert it exactly. But measurement noise gets amplified. The raw inversion was off by 4.4 points on average, and by up to 13 points in the towns. That's what ill-posed means. Many hidden maps fit the traces almost equally well, and small changes in the data cause large changes in the answer. The classic fix is regularisation: among the maps that fit, prefer ones where neighbours are similar. With a light smoothing penalty, the error fell to 2.2 points, and in the towns to 3.4. But smoothing has a price. At the market-town hot spots, the raw inversion was off by 2.5 points. Light smoothing made that 2.7, and heavy smoothing, 5.2. Sharp concentrations get blurred away. Other penalties encode other beliefs: hiding concentrated in a few places, or paths that are smooth with occasional breaks. Either way, the answer depends on the prior, so report it.

transcript.title: Other traces
transcript.text: Reconstruction gets stronger when several traces see different parts of the hidden map. Researchers have linked night-time lights, satellite imagery, and phone records to output, poverty and wealth, especially where official statistics are thin. None of these measures the hidden economy directly. They show how to anchor high-resolution traces with a few careful labels, and why you must test on regions the model never saw. For hiding, each trace needs a reason to respond to hidden activity, not just to activity in general.

transcript.title: Ways it fails
transcript.text: Spatial reconstruction can fail in at least five ways. Let's see some of them in our world. First, an ambiguous trace. Cash can mean hiding, or tourists, or distrust of banks. We added tourist cash at the port. The port's error doubled, from about five points to about ten. Second, a wrong operator. Suppose we believe rural districts withdraw 40 percent of their cash in town, when it's really 80. The error jumped to 11.6, up from 2.2. If we send 30 percent of the districts to the wrong town, the error rises to 4.3. Third, a wrong graph. We deleted 30 percent of the neighbour links used for smoothing. The error barely moved, 2.2 either way. Here, the operator mattered far more than the graph. Fourth, boundary mismatch: the traces and the benchmarks are counted over different regions. Fifth, process change: a reform or a new payment system changes how hiding becomes visible. And sixth, if you like, support failure: applying the model to districts unlike any surveyed one, which we met in the last video. Uncertainty in a reconstructed map has to include the operator, the graph and the prior, not only the noise.

transcript.title: Hold out whole regions
transcript.text: Now, validating spatial predictions. Suppose every district had a survey, and we want to know how well a model would do in a region it never saw. We compare four models: the plain average, a regression on the economic indicators, a random forest that also sees coordinates, and an average of the five nearest districts on the map. The usual check holds out random districts. The spatial check holds out whole blocks of the map, five regions in turn. Before the numbers, guess. Which model will lose the most when we switch to whole blocks? The map neighbours. With random holes, every test district has surveyed neighbours, and the error is 2.3. With whole blocks held out, it doubles, to 4.6. The forest's error grew too, to 2.1, up from 1.8. The regression on indicators lost the least: 1.9, up from 1.7. It relies on the economy, not on location, so it travelled best. Also check the leftovers. Moran's I of the errors was 0.58 for the map neighbours and 0.22 for the regression. A spatial pattern in the errors means something spatial was missed. And ask whether each target region lies inside the range of the training data. If it doesn't, the block check should say so.

transcript.title: Smooth gently
transcript.text: One more knob: smoothing a model's predictions over the graph. The regression's block-checked error was 1.9. Light smoothing brought it to 1.6. Heavy smoothing pushed it up to 3.8, because it erased real differences, including the step at the river. A strong Moran's I says neighbours are similar. It doesn't say they should be forced to be identical.

transcript.title: A small graph of regimes
transcript.text: The last idea of the module is reduction. A detailed spatial model can be expensive to simulate again and again. Can a small graph do the job? We follow the 160 districts for twenty years. That's 3,200 district-years, each a point in a space of hidden share, cash, digital payments, self-employment and location. Halfway through, the East adopts e-invoicing. The reduction has two stages. First, partition the space into a few regimes. Each regime becomes a node. Second, learn how districts move between regimes, as a transition table. Then score two things. Fidelity: does the small model reproduce the national trajectory? And reduction: with eight nodes instead of 160 districts, pairwise interactions shrink by 99.8 percent. A map grid is the obvious partition. But districts never move on the map, so the grid's transition table says nothing ever changes. It matched the national path at 93.7 percent. Economic regimes do better. Eight k-means regimes followed the path at 98.0 percent, and their transition model at 97.1. Why the gap? A transition table only knows the current regime, not the year. It spread the reform's sudden drop over two decades. Other partitions make other trade-offs. Covering the space evenly kept a rare regime where the hidden share averaged 39 percent. K-means merged it into a regime near 36. Adaptive splitting adds nodes where the map is most mixed. Always report fidelity and reduction together. And a transition between regimes describes what similar districts did. It's not a causal path.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Traces show where activity becomes visible. Working backwards is an inverse problem, and regularisation makes it stable at the cost of blurring. The observation operator can matter more than the graph. Get it wrong, and the map is wrong with confidence. Validate by holding out whole regions, check the errors for leftover structure, and smooth gently. A small graph of regimes can stand in for a detailed map, if you report both fidelity and reduction. In the lab, you'll reconstruct the Mainland from its cash traces, and build your own reduced graph. Next module: building the hidden economy from the bottom up. Agent-based simulation.

episodes.title: An executable theory
episodes.hook: A thousand invented traders, the same average threshold: a narrow spread keeps hidden trade at 2%, a slightly wider one takes it to everyone.
episodes.takeaway: Beliefs, not true audit rates, drive choices (30% hidden when firms know the rate, 36% or 20% when they believe otherwise). Complex contagion reached everyone on a clustered network and 1% on a random one; learning firms hid 28%, not the textbook 69%.

transcript.title: Same people, opposite outcomes
transcript.text: A thousand invented traders. Nobody is told to hide anything. Each one simply watches the others, and joins in once enough of them do. Give them thresholds that vary a little, and hidden trade never takes off. It stays with the two percent who started it. Make the thresholds vary a bit more, with the same average, and everyone ends up joining. Same people on average, opposite outcomes. To see effects like this, you have to let agents act and interact. That's agent-based simulation.

transcript.title: Three steps
transcript.text: Welcome to Module 7: simulating the hidden economy. I'm Teddy. In this video we'll build the idea of an agent-based model, design one from a question, and look at the rules agents use to decide: alone, in groups, and by learning.

transcript.title: What an agent-based model is
transcript.text: An agent-based simulation is an executable theory. Every agent has a state, information, a set of possible actions, and a rule for choosing among them. Agents can be people, households, firms, banks, platforms, or a tax office. They don't have to be identical. Differences are represented directly, not averaged away. Institutions decide which deals are allowed, taxed, reported, or visible. Totals like output or the hidden share are computed only after the agents have acted. The cycle repeats: agents observe, decide, interact, and the world updates. Whether everyone acts at once, or one after another, is part of the model, not a coding detail. Annual tax declarations fit agents acting together, once a year. Word of mouth and inspections fit agents acting one after another, each seeing what came before. How is this different from other tools? A microsimulation applies estimated transitions to individual records, usually without interaction. A system-dynamics model tracks aggregate stocks and flows. A game focuses on payoffs and equilibrium. An agent-based model can borrow from all three. Its defining feature is that heterogeneous agents and their interactions are actually executed. For the hidden economy, the key unit is often the transaction: its true value, its declared value, how it was paid, and whether the authority can see it. That separates breaking a rule from being unseen. A legal sale can be missing from statistics. A caught evasion is no longer hidden.

transcript.title: Start from a question
transcript.text: Start from a question, not from software. Does a higher audit rate reduce under-reporting? That needs a small population and a simple reporting rule. Does platform reporting change informal work, firm entry and revenue? That needs workers, firms, a platform, transactions, and feedback over time. Then make the design decisions in order: outputs, agents, states, information, actions, rules, interactions, institutions and observation, the evidence for calibration, and the experiments. Keep only the differences that matter for the mechanism. If income and tax morale drive reporting, let them vary. Don't simulate eye colour because a generator can. Begin with the smallest model that can answer the question, test it, and add a mechanism only when you can show it's missing. And describe it so others can rebuild it: who the agents are, what they know, what they can do, why they choose, who they meet, and how outcomes are measured.

transcript.title: Deciding alone
transcript.text: Now the decision rules. The classic starting point is expected utility: weigh the tax saved against the expected penalty, the moral cost, and the social cost. In our setup, the tax is 25 percent and the penalty adds 50 percent of the hidden amount. With no moral cost, hiding pays unless the audit chance is above one in three. But agents act on what they believe, not on the true rate. We gave 2,000 firms different moral costs and a true audit chance of 4 percent. If they know the true rate, they hide 30 percent of their income. If they believe it's 1 percent, they hide 36. After a visible campaign, believing it's 10 percent, they hide 20. People also have limited time and attention. They satisfice, use rules of thumb, or choose noisily, picking better options more often but not always. A noisy choice rule has a consistency parameter. In our firms, a perfectly consistent rule leads 36 percent to hide. As choices get noisier, that share drifts toward half. Noise can stand for real experimentation. It shouldn't hide a missing mechanism. Vary it, and check that conclusions don't depend on implausibly frequent mistakes. Choices under risk can also lean on a reference point. A penalty can feel like losing money already in hand, and a small audit chance can feel bigger or smaller than it is.

transcript.title: Thresholds and contagion
transcript.text: Decisions are made in groups. Peers carry information about audits, set norms, and make some actions easier. Invoice-free trade is easier when your suppliers already accept it. A threshold rule captures this. Each agent joins once the share of others doing it passes their personal threshold. Our thousand traders have thresholds averaging 30 percent, and two percent start. With a narrow spread, hidden trade stays at two percent. With a slightly wider spread, it reaches everyone. Here's the starkest version. A hundred agents with thresholds zero, one percent, two percent, and so on. Each one's joining triggers the next, and everyone joins. Change one agent's threshold from one percent to two, and the chain stops at the first person. Some behaviour needs reinforcement from several contacts. If a trader joins only after two neighbours have, it spread to everyone on a clustered network, and to about one percent on a random one. Simple contagion, needing just one contact, spread everywhere on both. So the network's shape matters, and so does the rule.

transcript.title: The communication rule
transcript.text: Beliefs spread too. Suppose 200 agents each hold a view on how acceptable undeclared work is, and they talk. Same starting views, three communication rules. With open averaging among neighbours, everyone converges to one shared view. If agents only listen to people who already think alike, the population splits into four separate camps. If one agent in ten never changes their mind, agreement never arrives. Views stay spread out for good. Agents learn from peers is not a model. The communication rule is the model.

transcript.title: Learning
transcript.text: Finally, learning. A simple learner keeps a value for each action and nudges it after every outcome. Hide and escape, and hiding looks better. Get caught, and it looks worse. With a 5 percent audit chance, the textbook answer says about 69 percent of our firms should hide. After thirty years of quarterly learning, 28 percent do. Learning is slow, and it depends on luck. Among firms with similar moral costs, every one that was never caught ended up hiding. Of those caught early, only about four in ten did. Evolutionary rules work one level up. Strategies that do well get copied, weak ones disappear, and mutation keeps adding new ones. A learned policy isn't free of assumptions. The reward, the actions, the exploration and the training world all encode a theory.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. An agent-based model is an executable theory: agents, information, actions, rules, interactions and institutions. Start from a question, keep only the differences that matter, and describe the model so it can be rebuilt. Beliefs differ from the truth, choices are noisy, thresholds create cascades, communication rules shape consensus, and learning depends on rewards and luck. In the lab, you'll set thresholds, networks and communication rules, and watch hidden trade spread or stall. Next video: from many small decisions to a whole economy, and the feedback that ties them together.

episodes.title: From micro to macro
episodes.hook: Saltmarsh, an invented town of 400 firms: nobody is told to hide, and about 31% of output goes unrecorded.
episodes.takeaway: A recession left hiding about a point higher two years after demand returned. At a 6% audit rate, a town that started with hiding common ended at 38% against 29%. Two calibrations with the same average disagreed completely about targeted audits.

transcript.title: Saltmarsh
transcript.text: This is Saltmarsh, an invented town of 400 firms and 2,000 households. We told nobody to hide. Each firm decides how much of its cash sales to declare. Card sales are always recorded. Hiding emerges anyway: about 31 percent of output goes unrecorded. And it's not spread evenly. Almost a quarter of the firms hide nothing at all, while one tenth of the firms account for over a third of the hidden sales. This video goes from small decisions to a whole economy, and follows the feedback that ties them together.

transcript.title: Three steps
transcript.text: Welcome back to Module 7. This is video two: from micro to macro. We'll look at the actors of a micro model, build Saltmarsh, and then watch what happens in a recession, under different audit rates, and after a reform.

transcript.title: The actors of a micro model
transcript.text: Start with households. A worker's choice depends on opportunity, not only taste. If everyone could take a good formal job and some refuse, the model confuses informality with preference. So job offers, skills, registration costs and family needs should limit what an agent can choose. Informal work can be survival, a side income, an entrepreneur's choice, or the employer's condition. Customers matter too. Some value a receipt or a warranty. Others prefer a discount. Model only the seller, and you miss the bargain that keeps hidden sales alive. Firms need a balance sheet: cash in from sales, cash out for wages, costs, taxes and penalties. Without it, a strategy can look attractive only because a cost was forgotten. A sale can be settled in two steps: first the economic terms, then the reporting terms. Is there an invoice, how much is declared, and through which channel? Who meets whom is a choice too. Random matching suits anonymous markets. Search lets buyers compare prices. Networks capture repeat relationships and trust. A platform can rank sellers, charge fees, and report sales. Tax-compliance simulations have a long history. They show that audits, memories of past audits, public goods and imitation can create lasting groups with very different reporting habits.

transcript.title: How the town works
transcript.text: Here's how Saltmarsh works. Every quarter, households buy from firms. A firm that sells without receipts can offer a discount, which attracts some customers. Each firm chooses how much cash revenue to declare. It weighs the tax, its perceived audit risk and the penalty, a moral cost, and what its peers are doing. Perceived risk rises after the firm's own audit, or after audits it sees in its group, and then fades. The moral cost grows with trust. Trust follows public services, and services are paid for by the revenue the town actually collects. The tax office sees what's declared, plus whatever its audits catch. We see everything, because the town is invented.

transcript.title: A pattern nobody typed in
transcript.text: Run it, and a pattern emerges that we never typed in. About 23 percent of firms declare everything. Most of the others hide more than a quarter of their sales. And 37 percent of all hidden sales come from firms that declare most of what they sell. A model that splits the town into a formal sector and an informal one would call those firms formal, and miss more than a third of the hiding. The line between seen and unseen runs through the same firm, sometimes through the same day's sales. There are three common ways to represent the sectors: fixed groups, groups that agents can switch between, or individual transactions. Only the last can show one firm reporting some sales and hiding others.

transcript.title: A recession and the feedback loop
transcript.text: Now the micro-macro loop. Hidden sales lower revenue. Lower revenue means weaker services. Weaker services lower trust, and lower trust makes hiding cheaper. Let's hit Saltmarsh with a recession. Demand drops by 15 percent for two years, and some workers lose their jobs and sell side services off the books. By the end of the recession, the hidden share is about three points above the path without one. Trust has fallen, and it recovers slowly. Two years after demand comes back, hiding is still about a point higher. The shock was temporary. Part of its effect wasn't. One more lesson from the same run. Revenue fell by 17 percent, while activity fell by 13. A drop in revenue isn't a measure of evasion. Keep true, declared and detected activity separate. Bigger macro models add banks, credit, prices, investment and a full government budget. The discipline stays the same: totals come from agents, and every flow has to balance.

transcript.title: When history matters
transcript.text: Feedback can also create tipping points. We ran Saltmarsh at many audit rates, starting once from a town where hiding is common, and once from a town where it's rare. At low audit rates, both towns end up in the same place. But in the middle, history matters. At a 6 percent audit rate, the town that started high hides 38 percent. The one that started low hides 29. At 10 percent, it's 17 against 10. Once hiding is normal, it takes more enforcement to undo it than it took to prevent it. That's why transition paths matter, not just end points. A reform can look weak for years, and then tip. Shocks and policies also differ in one way agents care about. They can prepare for an announced reform. They can't prepare for a surprise.

transcript.title: A reform, and two towns with one average
transcript.text: Now a reform. From quarter twenty, the largest quarter of firms must issue e-invoices, so every sale they make is recorded. A good experiment states the baseline, when the intervention starts, what it's compared with, the horizon, and how many random runs were averaged. We averaged several random towns for every scenario. The hidden share falls from 31 percent to 12. And the small firms, which were not reformed, hide less too: 23 percent of their sales instead of 37. Why? Their peers stopped hiding, and higher revenue raised trust. Turn those channels off, leaving only customers chasing discounts, and the small firms barely change. About one percent of the removed hidden sales moved to them. So the answer to reduce or displace depends on which mechanisms the model contains. That's a reason to test each mechanism against evidence. Here's a sharper warning. We calibrated two versions of Saltmarsh to the same average, both about 30 percent hidden. In one, moral costs are similar across firms. In the other, they vary a lot. Then we pointed every audit at the riskiest firms. In the first town, hiding collapsed to about two percent. In the second, it didn't fall at all. Validate at several levels. Check individual decisions, the spread of hidden shares, the networks and the totals. Then check how the model reacts to past shocks. Last, test it on policies that weren't used for calibration. Matching an average is not validation. Each mechanism needs evidence at the level where it works.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Micro models need constrained choices, both sides of every sale, and balance sheets. Totals are computed from agents. Feedback through revenue, services and trust can make a temporary shock leave a lasting mark, and can make history matter. Policy answers depend on the mechanisms included, and two models with the same average can disagree completely. Two habits carry over to any model. First, keep true, declared and detected activity apart. A fall in revenue isn't a measure of evasion. Second, watch the path, not only the end point. Once hiding is normal, undoing it takes more enforcement than preventing it did, and a reform can look weak for years before it tips. In the lab, you'll run your own town, hit it with a recession, and try to tip it back. Next video: models across levels, agents that learn or talk, and calibrating a model to data.

episodes.title: Multi-resolution, LLM agents, and a calibrated town
episodes.hook: Five of 256 settings of Saltmarsh fit its history. Double the audit rate and they disagree: hiding falls by 20 points, or by 26.
episodes.takeaway: Adding the honest share as a second target left one setting. Risk-score audits recovered most per audit (0.28) but left more hiding (35% against 30% at random). The peer version fit the past better and forecast worse; repeating last year's benchmark was off by 0.4.

transcript.title: Many settings, one history
transcript.text: We tried 256 different settings of Saltmarsh, our invented town. Five of them reproduce its hidden share to within two points. Same history, five models. Now double the audit rate. One model says hiding falls by 20 points. Another says by 26. Fitting the past doesn't pick one model. This video is about building models across levels, giving agents more flexible minds, and calibrating them honestly.

transcript.title: Three parts
transcript.text: Welcome back to Module 7. This is the last video of the module: multi-resolution models, learning and language-model agents, and a calibrated example.

transcript.title: Multi-resolution models
transcript.text: Economies are nested. Individuals sit in households and firms, which sit in sectors and regions, which sit inside national institutions. A multi-resolution model connects these levels without forcing one formalism on all of them. Individuals can be agents, supply chains a graph, sector demand an equation, and the government an optimiser. The feedback crosses levels. Individual hiding changes revenue. Revenue changes services and enforcement. Institutions change trust, and trust changes individual hiding. A hybrid is right when one mechanism needs individuals and another is fine as a total. Firms can be agents choosing how to report, while inflation arrives from an outside series and public services follow a budget equation. The interfaces must be explicit. If an unemployment rate affects workers, say when it's computed and who sees it. If a learned model predicts defaults, keep its output inside the firm's balance sheet. A tidy design has four layers: agents, interactions, institutions with observation, and analytics for calibration and prediction. Test each layer alone before joining them, and never count the same outcome twice.

transcript.title: Calibration across levels
transcript.text: Calibration can work bottom-up, from household, firm, audit or survey data. Top-down, from totals like output, revenue and a benchmark of the hidden share. Or both. Joint calibration needs weights for each target, and those weights are a choice. Put everything on the national total, and you can get a model that fits it with absurd agents. Back to our 256 settings. We varied two things: how strong moral costs are, and how much firms copy their peers. The five that fit the hidden share disagree about the town underneath. In one, 24 percent of firms are fully honest. In another, 38. One town has strong morals and heavy copying. Another has weak morals and little copying. Both produce the same total, so the total can't tell them apart. Add a second target, the share of fully honest firms, and only one setting is left. Distributions are evidence too. When data can't decide, report the whole set of acceptable models. Here, all five agree that more audits cut hiding sharply. They disagree on how much. That's the honest finding.

transcript.title: A learning auditor
transcript.text: Next, agents that learn. Instead of a fixed rule, a policy is updated from experience. What it learns depends on what it's rewarded for. Think of a learning tax office in Saltmarsh, choosing how to pick firms for audit. We compared three ways: at random, by a risk score from each firm's cash share, or by revisiting firms caught before. Per audit, the risk score recovers the most: about 0.28 units. Random audits recover 0.24. A learner rewarded for recovered tax per audit would choose the risk score. But in the long run, the town hides 35 percent under risk-based audits, against 30 under random ones. Random audits reach everyone's expectations, and total revenue ends up higher. Revisiting known evaders did worst on both counts: 0.17 per audit, and 39 percent hidden. And when everyone learns at once, firms adapting to the office and the office to the firms, the world keeps moving. Test learned policies outside the conditions they were trained in, and against simple rules. The lesson isn't that learning is bad. The reward has to measure what you actually want, over the horizon you care about.

transcript.title: Language-model agents
transcript.text: Large language models open another option: agents that read situations in words, remember stories, talk to each other, and choose with context. A language-model agent has a persona, a memory, a structured observation, a prompt, a list of permitted actions, and a validator. They can play different roles: deciding for varied personas, explaining choices in words, or handling only the few decisions that are hard to write as a rule. The model proposes. The simulation decides. The proposal is parsed into a fixed format. A validator rejects anything that breaks a budget, a balance or the rules. Only a permitted action is executed, and the prompt, the model version and the settings are logged. Researchers have used such agents to let concealment emerge without ever telling agents that evasion is the topic. That changes the question from how often to when. The risks are real. Answers can shift with wording, model version, temperature or memory. Populations of language agents can drift into their own conventions, or echo stereotypes from training data. Plausible isn't the same as valid. So use a fixed action schema, an accounting validator, version control, a memory policy, ablation tests, comparisons with human data, and cost control. And when the decision is a simple tax calculation, an equation is still better.

transcript.title: A calibrated example
transcript.text: Finally, a calibrated example from start to finish. We invented ten countries with a 25-year benchmark of the hidden share. A hidden process we know made the benchmark, with its own measurement error. Each country gets 100 agents in five villages, with self-employment, income, a tolerance for cheating, and sensitivity to audit risk. Each agent moves gradually toward the hidden share its situation favours. Two versions: private reasons only, or private reasons plus the village's average behaviour. We calibrated both on the first twenty years, and kept the last five for checking. The peer version fit the past better, with an average error of 1.5 points against 1.8. On the five held-out years, it did worse: 3.3 against 2.9. Both beat regressions on the same inputs, which were off by about five points. And simply repeating last year's benchmark was off by only 0.4. Why did the agents miss? The benchmark kept falling in the last years. Whatever drove that decline wasn't in the agents' world, so they had no reason to follow it. An agent model is for mechanisms and what-ifs. It doesn't have to win at next year's number, but you have to say so.

transcript.title: What-ifs and their assumptions
transcript.text: Now the what-ifs, from year 21, using the peer version. A stronger audit signal, by half: no effect at all. That's not a finding about audits. The audit signal barely changed in our data, so the calibration couldn't learn its effect and set it to zero. The scenario just repeats that assumption. Better services and trust, lowering tolerance for cheating: the hidden share fell by about 2 points. And even then, about two thirds of agents still hid more than 30 percent. Last, the peer weight, which country totals can barely identify. At the calibrated weight, the final hidden share is 38 percent. Without peers, 32. At three times the weight, 53. So any claim about social contagion here needs network, survey or experimental evidence, not just a good fit to totals. Every scenario inherits the calibration's blind spots. Before reporting a what-if, check whether the data could have taught the model that effect at all.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Multi-resolution models connect levels through explicit interfaces, layer by layer. Many settings can fit one history. Use distributions as targets, and report the set of acceptable models. Learning agents learn what they're rewarded for. Language-model agents propose, and the simulation validates. Calibrate on the past, check on held-out years, compare with simple baselines, and state what each scenario really assumes. In the lab, you'll calibrate a small town and try its what-ifs. Next module: designing policy against the hidden economy, when every choice has a cost and the truth is uncertain.

episodes.title: Optimal relative to what?
episodes.hook: Four policy packages, a thousand futures: services first wins on average, digital reporting wins in the worst tenth.
episodes.takeaway: Audit models trained on past audits found evaders 55% of the time; 6% random audits for learning lifted that to 64%. Three-year-old numbers made an adaptive rule overshoot by 8 points, and a method change in the same year made the audit effect look twice as large.

transcript.title: Four packages, a thousand futures
transcript.text: Four policy packages for our invented Mainland, each costing about the same. We ran each one through a thousand possible futures. On average, the package that funds services and formalisation wins. After ten years, it leaves about 15 percent of the economy hidden. But in the worst tenth of futures, a different package wins: the one that invests in digital reporting. Best is always best by some measure, under some assumptions. This module is about choosing policy when the truth is uncertain and every choice has a cost.

transcript.title: Four steps
transcript.text: Welcome to Module 8: designing policy against the non-observed economy. I'm Teddy. In this video: what counts as policy here, how to turn it into a decision problem, the kinds of uncertainty, the ways to optimise under them, and how to fit the models that predict a policy's effect.

transcript.title: Goals and instruments
transcript.text: Policy against the hidden economy is much more than audits and fines. It includes third-party reporting, e-invoicing, traceable payments, easier registration, simpler rules, social protection, public services and trust. And it can aim at four different things.
