Reducing the true amount of hidden activity. Formalising workers and firms. Making activity visible to the authorities. Or reducing harm, like protecting workers, even before full formalisation is possible. One instrument can help one goal and hurt another. Digital reporting can make activity visible without reducing it. An aggressive audit campaign can raise revenue while pushing vulnerable workers away and eroding trust. So we describe the state with several numbers: the true hidden share, how much the authority can observe, trust, and the wider context. And the policy with several instruments: audits, digital reporting, and services. A policy can be fixed, a schedule over years, or a rule that reacts to new data. And it has to respect budgets, capacity, law, fairness and risk.

transcript.title: Whom to audit
transcript.text: Take a classic decision: whom to audit. On paper, it's simple. Pick the firms with the highest expected recovery, until the budget runs out. But every number in that formula is uncertain. And one of them hides a trap: the risk estimates are learned from past audits, and past audits weren't random. We invented 2,000 firms in four sectors. One sector is the riskiest: more than half of its firms evade. But an old rule never audited it. A model trained on past audits finds an evader in 55 percent of its next 200 audits. That beats random audits, at 37. But only 27 percent of its picks come from the riskiest sector. It can't learn about firms it has never seen. Add six percent of audits chosen at random, just for learning. The next model finds an evader 64 percent of the time, almost as well as if we knew the true risks. And 85 percent of its picks now come from the riskiest sector. A little randomness buys a lot of knowledge.

transcript.title: Average, bad tail, worst case
transcript.text: Uncertainty comes from six places. The measurement itself. Unknown response coefficients. Which mechanism is right. How people adapt. Whether the policy is delivered as planned. And shocks from outside. Keep them apart. If the measured hidden share rises after a reform, it could mean more hiding, better detection, or a new method of measurement. Each calls for a different response. Our Mainland model has three instruments and three states: the hidden share, observability, and trust. Every response coefficient is uncertain, so each of the thousand futures draws its own, plus recessions and noise. The simplest criterion is the average outcome. Services first wins, at about 15 percent. Enforcement first gets 20, digital reporting 22, and the status quo 25. But averages hide bad tails. Look at the worst ten percent of futures. There, digital reporting does best, at 27 percent. Services first reaches 28, because it depends on an effect we're unsure about. Enforcement first reaches 33. In its single worst future, enforcement first ends at 48 percent. When trust collapses, heavy audits backfire. One caution about scenarios. Running more random seeds doesn't fix an equation that's wrong. The scenarios have to span the uncertainty that matters, including the mechanisms themselves. So report more than one number for every package: its average, its bad tail, and its worst case. A ranking that holds under all three is worth more than a win on any single one.

transcript.title: Robust choices and chance targets
transcript.text: That's the idea of robust optimisation: choose the policy whose worst plausible outcome is acceptable. It needs no probabilities, only a set of plausible values. Its danger is being too cautious, if that set includes combinations that can't happen together. A middle way protects against a range of possible distributions, not just one. That matters here, because a policy can change the very patterns it was trained on. Or set a chance constraint: the hidden share must end below 22 percent with high probability. Services first gets there in 72 percent of futures, enforcement in 59, digital reporting in 47, the status quo in 23. How high is high enough? Ninety percent? Ninety-five? That number is a policy choice, not a statistical constant.

transcript.title: Adaptive policy and late information
transcript.text: A fixed plan isn't always safest. A government can pilot, watch, and adjust. For example, raise audits when the hidden share is above target, and lower them when it's below. But the hidden share arrives late. We ran that rule three ways: with last year's number, with a one-year delay, and with a three-year delay. With fresh numbers, it overshot the target by about five points and used twelve audit-years. With a three-year delay, it overshot by eight, and used fifteen. It kept pushing long after the job was done. When the model is a simulation, the objective is a noisy black box. Start with a plain grid or random search, then re-test the finalists in many fresh futures. A clever optimiser can fail silently. And remember the practical limits. Instruments have start-up costs, delays and saturation. Assigning money to e-invoicing doesn't mean everyone adopts it, and assigning an audit doesn't mean it gets done. These limits belong inside the model, not in a footnote. A plan that ignores them will look better on paper than it does in the field.

transcript.title: Fitting the response model
transcript.text: All of this rests on a model of how the world responds to policy. Fitting the past is one question. Whether the policy's effect is identified, for the range you plan to use, is another. Here's a trap. In our invented history, audits rose in year six. In the same year, the statistics office changed its method, which made the measured hidden share three points lower. Calibrate without knowing that, and the model credits audits with the drop. It estimates an audit effect of 0.12, more than twice the true 0.05. Add a term for the method change, and the estimate falls to 0.08. Closer, but still off, because both changes happened in the same year. The data can't fully separate them. When a likelihood is out of reach, simulated moments, approximate Bayesian computation or synthetic likelihood can still fit a simulator. And always ask who could enter the data, and why an outcome was observed. Evaluate the model where decisions are made: near budget limits and near the points where the preferred policy changes. And treat published effects from other countries as ranges, not as universal constants.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Counter-NOE policy has four distinct goals, and instruments can help one while hurting another. Learned audit rules inherit past selection. A little random auditing fixes a lot. The best policy depends on the criterion: average, bad tail, worst case, or a chance target. Adaptive rules need timely information, and fitted effects need identification. In the lab, you'll choose a package for the Mainland and see how its ranking changes with the criterion. Next video: many objectives at once, which assumptions really matter, and a policy study from start to finish.

episodes.title: Many objectives, sensitivity, and an end-to-end policy study
episodes.hook: 145 affordable policy mixes, each run through a thousand futures: only 21 are not beaten on both cost and hidden share.
episodes.takeaway: Weights picked anything from the full budget to doing nothing. The services effect explained most of the spread (total index 0.45), and learning it first was worth about 1.8 points. Under digital reporting, detections rose while true hiding fell.

transcript.title: 145 mixes, 21 on the front
transcript.text: We tried every affordable mix of audits, digital reporting and services for the Mainland. There are 145 of them, each run through a thousand futures. Only 21 are not beaten on both cost and hidden share at once. Every other mix wastes money or leaves hiding on the table. Choosing among those 21 is not a calculation. It's a decision. This video is about making it well.

transcript.title: Three parts
transcript.text: Welcome back to Module 8. This is video two: many objectives, sensitivity, and a policy study from start to finish.

transcript.title: Many objectives
transcript.text: A government cares about many things at once: hidden activity, revenue, worker protection, jobs, the burden on small firms, fair auditing, privacy, trust, and regional equity. One policy dominates another if it's no worse on every objective and better on at least one. The undominated policies form the Pareto front. The front removes waste. It doesn't pick a winner. On our front, spending moves the hidden share from 32 percent with no policy at all down to 12 at the full budget. The early steps buy the most. A weighted sum is the easy way to pick one. But watch the weights. Put a fifth of the weight on cost, and you choose the full-budget mix. Half the weight, and you choose light audits only. Most of the weight on cost, and you choose to do nothing. Small changes in weights, completely different policies. And weighted sums can miss parts of a front that isn't convex. So show the weights you used, and check how far they can move before the choice changes. If a small shift flips the answer, say so. A limit is often clearer. Minimise hidden activity, subject to trust staying at least one half and the cost at most 0.8. That picks moderate audits plus services, ending near 16 percent. Strict priorities, targets with allowed deviations, and evolutionary search for messy simulated fronts are other options. Choose the method that matches how the objectives are actually stated.

transcript.title: Constraints, horizon, combinations
transcript.text: Set the objectives before running anything, and don't choose weights after seeing which policy they favour. Fairness can be a constraint, like a cap on the difference in audit rates between regions. But equal rates aren't automatically fair if risk differs. The definition has to follow the purpose and the law. Some things shouldn't be traded at all. If no revenue gain can justify a privacy violation, privacy is a constraint, not an objective. The same goes for due process and minimum services. The horizon matters too. Some instruments pay back quickly, others need years of investment first. State the horizon and the discounting, and check that the choice survives other reasonable ones. And look for combinations. Digital records make audits sharper. Services make digital adoption easier. Some pairs work better together, and some work against each other. When you present results, show a few named packages, not hundreds of points. For each one: the average, the bad tail, the cost, who bears it, and the assumptions under which it stops being the best choice.

transcript.title: Sensitivity analysis
transcript.text: Next, sensitivity analysis. Uncertainty analysis describes the spread of outcomes. Sensitivity analysis asks which assumptions create it. Local derivatives are quick but see only a neighbourhood. Changing one input at a time is easy to explain, but misses interactions. Screening methods cheaply find the inputs worth a closer look. Global methods vary everything at once over its plausible range, and split the output's variance into contributions. The first-order index counts an input alone. The total index adds all its interactions. For the robust policy, the services effect explains the most, with a total index of 0.45. The audit effect follows, at 0.35, then the baseline drift, at 0.13. The first-order indices add up to only about 0.8. The rest comes from interactions, which a one-at-a-time analysis would never see. Use good sampling, check that the indices have converged, and don't choose the ranges after seeing the results. A ranking of inputs is not a ranking of causes. Beyond parameters, change the model itself: different decision rules for agents, different peer networks, a different benchmark. Some assumptions can't be tested by sweeping a number. And remember equifinality from Module 7. Test every candidate policy across all the calibrations that fit the data, not just the one that fits best.

transcript.title: Decision sensitivity and the value of information
transcript.text: But the question that matters for policy is simpler. Does the recommended policy change? We varied the services effect alone. If it's essentially zero, enforcement first wins. At small values, the robust mix wins, then the mix that's best on average. From a modest value upward, services first wins. So the decision hinges on one number we don't know well. That tells you where to spend research money. If we could learn the services effect before choosing, the expected hidden share would fall by about 1.8 points. Learning the audit effect is worth 0.7. Learning the direct effect of digital reporting, almost nothing. Run the pilot that could change your mind. And turn the influential quantities into monitoring indicators, with stopping rules written down in advance. A sensitivity analysis that ends with a table of indices is only half done. The useful ending is a sentence a decision maker can act on: which number to learn, how to learn it, and what you'd do with each answer.

transcript.title: The study, end to end
transcript.text: Now the whole study, end to end. The best mix on average spends on light audits and lots of services, and ends near 12 percent. Its worst tenth reaches 23. The robust mix adds a little digital reporting and more audits. Its average is a bit worse, near 13.5. Its worst tenth is better, at 22. And the knee of the front, where extra money starts buying much less, is audits alone at 40 percent of the budget, ending near 21 percent. One more lesson from the digital package. As observability rises, the part of hiding that the authority can see grows from 12 points to 18, while true hiding falls from 27 to 22. Read the rising detections as rising hiding, and you'd cancel a policy that's working. Report true, observed and unseen separately. All of these numbers come from an invented teaching model, not from real policy effects. Their value is in the workflow they demonstrate.

transcript.title: From model to study
transcript.text: Finally, turn the model into a study. First, pilot in a few regions, varying the instruments that drive the uncertainty, and measure adoption, appeals, survival, jobs, trust and payment channels. Second, recalibrate an ensemble of models with the pilot data, and prefer policies that stay near the front under all of them. A policy that's optimal only under one fragile equation shouldn't be scaled up. Third, implement adaptively, with the rules, indicators and review dates announced in advance. Adapting doesn't mean changing the objective after seeing the results. And communicate honestly. One package minimises the average, another the bad tail, a third balances cost, trust and hiding. Show the ranges and the assumptions. The choice belongs to the public. Each step leaves a record of what was assumed, what was tested and what was decided. That record lets someone else check the study, or redo it when new data arrive.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. The Pareto front removes waste. Weights, limits and priorities choose, and the method should match how the goals are stated. Global sensitivity finds the assumptions behind the spread. Decision sensitivity asks whether the recommendation changes, and the value of information says what to learn next. Report true, observed and unseen activity separately, and move from model to pilot to adaptive policy. In the lab, you'll explore the front, change the weights and limits, and run a sensitivity analysis on your favourite package. Next and final module: a practical guide, from a question to a defensible answer.

episodes.title: From a question to an estimand
episodes.hook: One invented e-invoicing reform, 3,000 firms, six correct answers to the question “does it work?”.
episodes.takeaway: Write the estimand first: population, outcome, intervention, comparator, horizon and summary. An estimand limited to eligible firms missed the small firms' slight rise in hiding and the closures above the size threshold.

transcript.title: One reform, six answers
transcript.text: Does e-invoicing reduce the hidden economy? We invented a reform for 3,000 firms, and got six different answers. All of them correct. Declared sales of the firms that must e-invoice rose by 11 percent. Their hidden share fell from 20 percent to 11. The whole economy's fell from 22 to 15. Revenue rose by about 10 percent. Detected hidden sales rose by 46 percent, because invoices make hiding easier to catch. And among firms just above the size threshold, almost four in a hundred more closed. Six questions, six answers. A study has to say which question it answers before it computes anything. That's where this final module begins.

transcript.title: Two videos
transcript.text: Welcome to Module 9, the last module of the course: a practical guide to research on the non-observed economy. I'm Teddy. This video goes from a vague question to a precise target. The next one covers choosing models, validating them, and reporting.

transcript.title: A fixed order
transcript.text: A credible study runs in a fixed order. The question and its intended use define the target quantity. The target decides which evidence matters. The evidence limits the candidate models. Validation decides which conclusions survive. And reporting turns them into outputs people can use. Reverse that order, and the study weakens. Starting with we'll use a neural network, or we'll build a simulation, puts a favourite method in place of a defined task. Explaining, predicting and estimating an effect are different goals. A model that explains an association is judged one way. A forecasting model is judged another way. And a model that measures a policy's effect is judged a third way. The bridge is the estimand: the exact quantity the study is trying to learn. Write it down before choosing any estimator.

transcript.title: A topic is not a task
transcript.text: Studying tax evasion is a topic, not a task. Estimating the average undeclared share among registered retail firms in a given year is a measurement task. Ranking firms by expected recoverable tax for the next audit cycle is a detection task. Estimating the two-year effect of e-invoicing on eligible small firms is a causal task. Six task types cover most of the field: measurement, detection, forecasting, causal evaluation, simulation, and policy design. Each produces a different output: a level, a ranking, a trajectory, an effect, a generated distribution, or a portfolio. A project can contain several, but one should be primary, because each is judged differently. Measurement against evidence and accounting. Forecasts against later data. Scenarios on the credibility of their assumptions. A simple task card keeps it honest: the question, the audience, the output, the estimand, the data, the model, the validation, and the reporting. In that order. Fill in the card before the analysis starts, and keep it. When the results arrive, it shows whether the study answered the question it set out to answer.

transcript.title: Audience and the cost of error
transcript.text: Who will use the result matters. A statistics office needs an aggregate consistent with the accounts, with metadata and revision rules. A tax office needs a ranking that supports human review, with error rates and an audit trail. So does the cost of error. A country-level estimate that's off by two points may be fine for comparing countries, and serious for fiscal planning. Repurpose that country model to flag individual firms, and the error is no longer two points. It's a category mistake. A relationship among countries doesn't identify which firm is hiding. Write the output down precisely: a level, a probability, a distribution, a ranking. And state how often it updates, and how long it should live. If the data arrive a year late, a current-year number is a nowcast, not a measurement. Interpretability needs differ too. A statistics office may need every assumption visible. A tax office needs reasons a human reviewer can check, firm by firm. One question helps before any data work: what would the user do differently if the number came out high, or low? If nothing would change, the question needs more work before the data does.

transcript.title: Production, compliance, observability
transcript.text: Next, the concepts. Separate three properties of any activity. Is it production, inside the accounting boundary? Does it comply with the rules? And can the responsible institution observe it? A compliant activity can be unobserved, through gaps in statistics. A non-compliant one can be observed, once it's detected. So unobserved needs three more words: by whom, when, and for what purpose. Choose the unit to match the claim: transactions, workers, firms, regions, or country-years. Aggregating a firm into formal or informal loses the firm that does both. Fix the time basis: reference period, frequency, prices, data vintage, flows or stocks. And always state the denominator. In Module 1, one invented town's hidden economy was 15, 18 or 8 percent, depending on the definition and the denominator. State the benchmark's status too. Survey, audit, administrative, calibrated, or the output of another model. A flexible model trained on a model-based series is a model of a model. A handy test is one example in and one example out for every boundary. An undeclared repair job is in. An undeclared bank balance is not current production. Unpaid care is outside the usual production boundary, valuable as it is. Write each of these choices on the task card, so a reader can check them without guessing.

transcript.title: Building the estimand
transcript.text: Now turn a policy question into an estimand. Take our reform. Which population: all firms, or only those required to e-invoice? Which outcome: declared sales, true hidden sales, detected cases, revenue, or survival? Compared with what: no reform, or the old paper invoices? Over what horizon: a month, a year, five years? And summarised how: a mean, a share, a distribution? Fix all of these, and the question has one answer. Leave them open, and our six numbers all compete to be the effect. Keep three layers apart. The theoretical estimand is what you care about, like the true hidden share of eligible firms. The empirical estimand is what the data can identify under assumptions, like the gap between invoices and audit findings. The estimator is the procedure that computes it. For observational data, describe the experiment you wish you could run: who is eligible, what each group receives, when follow-up starts, and what's measured. Formalisation isn't an intervention until you say who gets what, how much, when, and compared with what. Causal diagrams help expose the assumptions that link the data to an effect. But a diagram doesn't replace knowing how the institution actually works. A written estimand also helps readers. They can see at once whether your number answers their question, or a nearby one.

transcript.title: Who is counted
transcript.text: Defining the population also decides what you can see. In our reform, the small firms that weren't required to e-invoice hid slightly more afterwards, about one point more, as some activity moved to them. An estimand limited to eligible firms would never notice. An economy-wide one would, but would mix that displacement with the main effect. The same goes for closures. If firms just above the threshold close, their hidden sales vanish from the eligible group, and the average can improve for the wrong reason. Survival belongs in the outcome list. So list every group a reform can touch, including firms just outside it, and say which of them your estimand counts. Most disagreements about whether a policy worked are disagreements about the estimand.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Question, estimand, evidence, models, validation, reporting. In that order. Name the task type and the audience, and price the errors. State production, compliance and observability, the observer, the unit, the time basis and the denominator. Turn every policy question into a population, an outcome, an intervention, a comparator, a horizon and a summary, before estimating anything. In the lab, you'll fill in a task card and an estimand card, and the lab will flag the common gaps. Next and final video: choosing models, validating them honestly, and reporting what you found.

episodes.title: Choose, validate, report
episodes.hook: The best of 300 specifications scored 2.9 by cross-validation, 3.35 on fresh countries, and 3.7 when the whole selection was checked.
episodes.takeaway: A pooled 90% interval covered 95% overall but 80% in the noisiest countries. Across 36 reasonable analyses the estimate ran from 19.8% to 22.3% (truth 20.4%), and the choice of benchmark explained 57% of the spread.

transcript.title: The best of 300
transcript.text: We gave 40 invented countries 22 possible predictors, only two of them real, and tried 300 model specifications. The best one, chosen by cross-validation, was off by 2.9 points. On fresh countries from the same world, it was off by 3.35. When the whole selection was repeated inside an outer check, the honest estimate was 3.7. Pick a winner and test it on the same data, and the winner looks better than it is. This last video is about choosing, validating and reporting honestly.

transcript.title: Three parts
transcript.text: Welcome back to Module 9. This is the final video of the course: choose, validate, report.

transcript.title: Readiness and candidates
transcript.text: Before models, check the data. For each source: coverage, timing, linkage, definitions, quality and access. A readiness check can say go, or say collect better data first. Where registers, invoices or payment data are thin, newer traces like night lights, phone records or platform data can help, but only with anchors, triangulation and honest benchmark uncertainty. Teaching data like ours are complete and reproducible. Real data are partial, revised and selected. Write down who could enter each dataset, and why each outcome was observed. Then choose a small candidate set: a transparent baseline, a model that matches the theory, and one flexible model. Baseline first, always. In Modules 5 and 7, simply repeating last year's number was hard to beat. The details often matter more than the algorithm: representation, data quality, leakage, the objective, and how you evaluate. Write down which checks failed, too. A model that couldn't be built is a finding about the data, and it saves the next team time.

transcript.title: Selection without self-deception
transcript.text: Now selection. Our 300 specifications had cross-validation errors from 2.9 up to about 4.7. The winner did contain both real predictors, plus two pieces of noise. Its reported score was the best of many tries on the same folds, so luck was built in. On fresh data it lost almost half a point. The fix is nesting. Tune and select inside an inner loop, and score the whole procedure on data the selection never touched. Report every specification you tried, not only the winner. Many models can fit about equally well while relying on different variables. That's the Rashomon effect, a cousin of the equifinality we met in Module 7. Report the range of stories, not one importance ranking. Avoid automatic stepwise selection, and keep a model card: purpose, data, candidates, baseline, tuning, assumptions, intended use, expected failures, and the uncertainty method. Information criteria, regularisation and model averaging are all reasonable ways to choose. What matters is that the choice happens inside the validation, not after a look at the test results. A quick test for any choice of model: could you have written the selection rule down before seeing the data? If not, the score you report includes some of your own searching.

transcript.title: Validation
transcript.text: Validation checks the whole procedure, from data preparation to thresholds, for its intended use. Test on later years, on other places, or in another institution, depending on how the model will travel. Random audits are unusually valuable here, because who gets audited doesn't depend on earlier rules. And when you validate someone else's model on new data, reproduce it exactly before changing anything. Document how leakage was prevented. Say how the data were resampled and how tuning was done. And state how far you claim the result generalises. Validate at the level of the claim. An aggregate model is checked against aggregates. A firm-level ranking is checked against firm-level outcomes, counting both false alarms and missed cases. And keep the final evaluation data untouched until the very end. Every peek turns test data into training data. If the model will be used in another place or another year, test it there before trusting it there. A score earned on familiar data says little about unfamiliar ones.

transcript.title: Uncertainty and coverage
transcript.text: Uncertainty has six sources: the measurement, the sample, the parameters, the model's form, the future, and how the result will be used. A standard error covers only part of that. Here's a subtle one. We built a 90 percent interval for next year's benchmark in 12 invented countries, calibrated on all of them together. Overall, it covered the truth 95 percent of the time. But in the three noisiest countries, only 80 percent. In the nine calmer ones, every time. Calibrating each country separately adapts the widths, from under one point to about seven. But with only ten years per country, one fell to 60 percent coverage. Report coverage by subgroup, and say how much data stands behind each interval. And watch for drift after deployment. A model can change the very behaviour it measures. Bootstrap the whole procedure to capture sampling variation. For panels and maps, resample whole countries or regions, not single rows, or the uncertainty will look smaller than it is. Even intervals with formal guarantees assume the future resembles the calibration data. A structural break isn't fixed by a cleverer interval. It's found by monitoring.

transcript.title: The multiverse
transcript.text: There's another kind of uncertainty: the choices the analyst makes. So run the multiverse. Repeat the analysis across every reasonable combination of choices. We estimated one invented country's hidden share for next year with three benchmark series, three history windows, and two models, one of them with three predictor sets. That's 36 reasonable analyses. They range from about 19.8 percent to 22.3. The true value was 20.4. And which choice mattered? The benchmark series explained 57 percent of the spread. The history window, 21. The predictors, 6. The model, almost nothing. That's worth knowing before collecting anything new. Here, settling which benchmark to trust would narrow the range far more than any change of model. The choice you argue about least can matter most. Show the whole multiverse.

transcript.title: Reporting
transcript.text: Finally, reporting. Keep the chain visible: the question, the estimand, the evidence, the model, the validation, and the uncertainty. A number without that chain is an assertion. Share a reproducibility package: code, data or access instructions, software versions, and random seeds, so someone else can get the same numbers. Separate what the evidence directly supports from what depends on model assumptions. And give both absolute and relative changes. A fall from 20 percent to 15 is five points, and also a quarter. If the result will guide action on people or firms, report errors by subgroup, the proxies the model relies on, who reviews its outputs, and how decisions can be appealed. For decision makers, add a one-page summary: what was asked, what was found, how sure we are, what would change the conclusion, and what should be measured next. And pre-register what you can: the estimand, the validation design and the main comparison, before seeing any results. It's the simplest protection against fooling yourself. Finally, say what the study cannot tell you. A clear list of limits makes the rest of the report more credible, not less.

transcript.title: The course in one view
transcript.text: Let's recap this video. Check data readiness, start from baselines, nest your selection, validate the whole procedure, report coverage by subgroup, and run the multiverse. And that's the course. We defined the non-observed economy, built theory and data around it, estimated and forecast it, mapped it, simulated it, designed policy against it, and turned it all into a research practice. Every number in these videos came from invented worlds we built, so we could check our methods against a truth. Real studies don't get that luxury, which is exactly why the habits matter. If you remember one thing, make it the order: question, estimand, evidence, model, validation, report. The decks, labs and transcripts for every module are on the course page. In the last lab, you'll design a complete study and get a report card. Thank you for learning with me. I'm Teddy. Go look for what's hidden, carefully.

labs.title: Lantern Bay's observers
labs.text: Switch the tax office, the statistics office and a card company on and off over an invented town, and see what each one records. Sort five producers into the five components, then change the definition and the denominator and watch the size of the non-observed economy move.
labs.intro: The town is our own invented Lantern Bay (the same numbers as in the videos), computed in your browser. Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Observers, components, definitions and denominators in an invented town.

labs.title: Forty countries
labs.text: Build forty invented countries, train a simple theory-guided model and a flexible one on a published estimate, and switch between random and country splits and between scoring against the estimate and against the truth. Then switch on a payments reform.
labs.intro: The countries are simulated in your browser (a hidden share driven by institutions, taxes and payments, and a published estimate that leans on cash). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Random versus country splits, estimate versus truth, and a reform that changes what is observed.

labs.title: The audit game
labs.text: Play an inspection game between a tax office and learning firms: change the fine, the audit cost and how noisy the firms are, and watch who adapts. Then sweep the audit rate up and down in a population that copies its neighbours.
labs.intro: Both games run in your browser with stylised payoffs (read the logic, not the levels). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: An inspection game with learning firms, and tipping when people copy each other.

labs.title: Estimate the Archipelago
labs.text: Fit a linear model with and without a logistic link, grow a decision tree question by question, choose the number of neighbours, and ask for 90% ranges. Every estimate is scored on countries the models never saw, against the truth.
labs.intro: The Archipelago is simulated in your browser (thirty countries with a careful benchmark, twenty to estimate). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Linear models, trees and neighbours on invented countries, with ranges you can test.

labs.title: The forecast desk
labs.text: Nowcast the hidden share of thirty invented countries with persistence, a regression on levels or anchor-and-update. Change how much history each sees, switch the digital-payments shift, the recession and the reform on and off, compare an honest rolling check with random held-out quarters, and watch the drift alarms.
labs.intro: The countries are simulated in your browser (a benchmark that covers a year and is published a year later, and quarterly indicators). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Persistence, regressions and anchor-and-update through three kinds of drift, checked honestly.

labs.title: The night atlas
labs.text: Explore an invented country of 160 hexagonal districts with 40 surveys. Choose who counts as a neighbour, estimate the unsurveyed districts, smooth across or within a river, test for spatial structure with shuffles, and hunt for hot spots, real and false.
labs.intro: The map is simulated in your browser (a river, a smuggling corridor, two market towns, hills). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Neighbours, smoothing, borders, Moran's I and false hot spots on an invented map.

labs.title: Town in silico
labs.text: Run a small agent-based town of 300 invented firms. Change the audit rate, how much firms copy their peers and how much their moral costs vary, add a recession or e-invoicing, and look for lasting marks and tipping points.
labs.intro: A small version of the videos' Saltmarsh, simulated in your browser. Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Peer effects, trust feedback, recessions, reforms and tipping points in an invented town.

labs.title: The policy room
labs.text: Spend a yearly budget on audits, digital reporting and services for an invented country, judged across 300 futures by the average, the worst tenth and the chance of reaching a target. Find the Pareto front, then run a pilot that pins an uncertain effect and see the decision change.
labs.intro: The course's ten-year teaching model, run in your browser. An invented model, not real policy effects. Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Criteria under uncertainty, a Pareto front and the value of a pilot.

labs.title: Study designer
labs.text: Fill in a task and estimand card that flags what does not fit together, then try up to 300 model specifications on forty invented countries and see how picking the best flatters it, and how nesting the selection gives an honest estimate.
labs.intro: Everything runs in your browser. Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: A self-checking study card, and selection optimism with and without nesting.
